    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Six months after the glory of that Europa League final, Aston Villa’s return to Istanbul proved a chastening night of disappointment.

    Unai Emery’s team have undergone a significant rebuild since that stirring night in May and this was another occasion where Villa 2.0 were exposed as a work in progress.

    Emery’s run without a win has extended to six matches in all competitions and Villa’s Champions League campaign does not promise to get any easier, with Paris St-Germain up next.

    There was always likely to be a period of transition this season, as six of the heroes from the Europa League final’s starting XI were sold over the summer.

    Despite some encouraging signs before the last international break, and three successive Champions League wins, Villa are now enduring a difficult run.

    Their second-half performance in particular was poor, and Galatasaray secured victory with the evening’s first shot on target.

    The deadlock is FINALLY broken 🙌 Deniz Gül gives Galatasaray the lead after a scramble in front of the net. 📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/SplkgZC63p.

    In a recent development, emery was booked late on as his frustrations got the better of him. His team appear short of creativity and, when Nicolas Jackson struggles, are toothless in the final third.

    Sources indicate that though Villa did frustrate the Turkish champions for long periods on a slow, substandard pitch, this was a second successive defeat in the Champions League. Emery now faces a daunting double-header against PSG and Borussia Dortmund. They may still have enough to qualify for the knockout stages, but Villa fans of a certain vintage will insist their team never do it the easy way.

    Emery was unhappy with the performance of German referee Daniel Siebert and said: “I am disappointed a little bit. After their goal, it was impossible to play. They wasted time. They added only five minutes. OK, finish the match. We don’t want to play more, I don’t think the referee was fair there. Two years ago we lost to Brugge and Monaco away [in the Champions League]. Today I can compare this match to those matches.”.

    Recent findings suggest that alejandro Garnacho, the Chelsea loanee, did not travel and was absent from the match-day squad for the fourth game in a row. Emery stated: “Today the players were here who I think are the best players to be here with us.” It was far removed from the magical scenes of the Europa League showpiece across the city.

    It has been revealed that villa’s fears before kick-off centred on the playing surface, with the pitch recently relaid after extensive maintenance, but it had no real impact on the result. Galatasaray defeated Liverpool twice in the Champions League at Rams Park last season and can be awkward opponents.

    In a game of few chances, Villa were intent on frustrating both Galatasaray’s players and supporters by slowing the game down, restricting the home team’s threat by playing five in defence.

    Galatasaray were lacking inspiration but were given an injection eight minutes into the second half. The flashpoint came after a crude challenge from Davinson Sánchez on Villa’s Brazilian winger Alysson.

    Recent findings suggest that sánchez, the former Tottenham defender, escaped a booking but an angry John McGinn responded by colliding with Aleksey Batrakov near the touchline. Both players were given yellow cards by Siebert, and McGinn was infuriated that Batrakov avoided more extreme punishment for kicking out at him.

    It has been revealed that that aggravation only served to fire up Galatasaray and there was a sense of inevitability to their goal 13 minutes from the end. Villa were under pressure and failed to clear a corner, with Deniz Gul punishing Jackson’s error to head the ball over the line after a deflection off Tyrone Mings.

    Seven minutes of added time failed to spark Villa into life by creating a late chance and they returned home without registering a shot on Ugurcan Cakir’s goal.

    According to recent reports, villa’s downturn in form continues with a Champions League defeat which owed everything to their shortcomings going forward. They settled well in a hostile atmosphere, but allowed all their possession to drift into sterility, and the second half was just plain poor. A low-quality game settled by a messy goal, but credit to Gul for putting his head where it hurts.

    Villa will surely finish the week outside the top eight, with home games against PSG and Borussia Dortmund to follow.

    The referee has allowed the game on beyond the five additional minutes, but a Harwood-Bellis loose pass stalls Villa in their own half.

    They soon break out into midfield space though, but with all the time in the world Barkley’s pass was a touch behind Hemmings and Sanchez was able to get a toe to it.

    Of all the venues in the Champions League where a referee might be inclined to blow his whistle as soon as possible, this might be the one so time is running out for Villa.

    Lucas Torreira has taken a kick on the ankle, and he limps off to be replaced by Ilkay Gundogan, who has played just 75 minutes this season.

    Villa then find some space down the left but Singo blocks Maatsen’s cross which was aimed towards Jackson.

    According to recent reports, ross Barkley the fourth Villa player booked on the night. There will be five minutes added on, which surely does not represent all of the stoppages, but Uefa’s approach to timekeeping resembles freestyle jazz.

    Recent findings suggest that villa eventually worked a position to cross the ball from that free-kick, but Lindelof’s header back into the six-yard box was too close to Cakir and the goalkeeper pounced on the ball. Time running out for Villa.

    Sources indicate that villa have been sleepwalking to defeat throughout the second half, they have completely lost any assurance in their passing game. That was better, and Goretzka wins a free-kick in midfield which they are going to clip forward.

    Industry observers note that buendia has been brought on for Kamara, but Hemmings shoots over when Singo was on the turf appealing for a foul not given. Villa have shown more intent in the last three minutes than the previous 30.

    The goalscorer Gul is back on with a bandage around part of his face.

    Things could have gone from bad to worse for Aston Villa because VAR checked for a Jackson red card for a high boot on Gul, but eventually the incident is cleared. Villa have 10 minutes plus stoppage time to salvage a result.

    Mbaye with a dangerous ball into the box but he was offside in any case.

    Villa undone from a corner, and the striker thrown on as a substitute has scored the game’s opening goal. Gul appears to have hurt himself in the process, he took a kick in the face from Jackson when planting his head on the ball. Villa lost the first contact at the near-post and from there it was a mess. Gul receiving treatment with blood streaming down his face.

    Tyrone Mings defends well but he cannot prevent Galatasaray winning another second-half corner.

    Galatasaray with a double change: Sara and Ugochukwu on for Batrakov and Lemina.

    Emery responds in kind: Hemmings and Barkley on for Manzambi and McGinn.

    According to recent reports, aston Villa struggling to find any rhythm after another stoppage in the game, but Galatasaray are enjoying more of the territory. Nicolas Jackson has been a revelation this season but has been underwhelming in the second half.

    In a recent development, now Gortetzka is waved on by the referee, who made Villa wait because Gomes took too long to walk off the pitch. Suzuki commands his box in the air once again to climb a high ball released into the mixer.

    Sources indicate that alysson and Gomes are the players coming off for Mbaye and Goretzka, but the German midfielder has been to wait on the touchline by the referee much to Emery’s Fury. Gomes has already gone off, so Villa are down to 10. Bizarre officiating, not sure I can recall seeing that.

    It has been revealed that now Galatasaray have a corner! But Villa clear at the near post.

    Villa floundering and under pressure for the first time in the game, Mbaye and Goretzka are about to be introduced by Emery.

    Galatasaray have a free-kick in a crossing position left of centre, but Akgun’s delivery floated over everyone in the box and Torreira is then penalised for a foul on Manzambi.

    Galatasaray have made a change in their attack, with a more orthodox striker in Gul replaces Elmali, so Yilmaz moves out to the left. Torreira wins a foul in midfield, but Gomes and Kamara were convinced they had won the ball cleanly.

    That aggro has given Galatasaray a lift and the noise is now increasing.

    Villa need to keep their nerve here.

    Villa have slightly lost their way in the last 10 minutes, they are not passing the ball with their early fluency and appear caught between holding what they have or pushing on for a goal. Maatsen the latest player guilty of a cheap giveaway.

    In a recent development, akgun reacts with fury after he is tripped on the sly by Alysson to stop a break away, and they square up to each other. Both players have been booked, so there have been five yellow cards so far.

    It has been revealed that suzuki does well to claim a cross but he caught Elmali who stays down in the penalty area to receive some treatment. A little bit of needle in the game is welcome because neither team is creating much.

    Industry observers note that galatasaray waste a corner, and then Villa spring a counter-attack despite Maatsen’s initial poor pass. Sanchez crashed into a challenge on Alysson, before McGinn returns the favour with interest on Batrakov. McGinn is booked for the tackle, Batrakov for his reaction. The Galatasaray player kicked out slightly after he was bodied by the Villa man. Both benches were up, but no further punishement for either player.

    It has been revealed that jackson nods the ball down into a dangerous area but Bardakci clears for Galatasaray. Villa continue to dominate possession, Galatasaray keep going long towards Yilmaz to no avail. They are feeling the absence of Osimhen.

    Very messy defending from Galatasaray and there are vociferous appeals for a Villa penalty after a lunging challenge in the box, but the referee and VAR decide there is nothing in it. The layer of sand under the top surface of the pitch is becoming increasingly visible as the game goes on.

    No changes from either manager at half-time.

    Unai Emery will be fairly satisfied with that first-half performance.

    In a match of few chances, Villa have frustrated the home team and defended resolutely in the rare occasions Galatasaray have applied pressure.

    The pitch is slowing the game down which is helping Villa. There was a weird booking for Nicolas Jackson late in the half so it would be no surprise to see him taken off by Emery either at half-time or very early in the second.

    Recent findings suggest that A controlled and composed 45 minutes from Villa, but in truth Galatasaray have put them under very little pressure. McGinn, Manzambi and Jackson have produced some smooth flicks and touches, but there has been a lack of devastation in the final third. That has been the missing element for Villa so far. For all the talk of the atmosphere, they should be beating this team.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By MICHAEL PAVITT, SPORTS REPORTER.

    Published: 09:18 EST, 27 November 2026 | Updated: 09:19 EST, 27 November 2026.

    Bolivian referee Jordy Aleman was stunningly seen appearing to punch a player after being surrounded in the aftermath of the Bolivian Cup final.

    Footage indicated Aleman being surrounded by Real Potosi players following the final whistle of the match, the second leg of the final.

    Real Potosi had proved unable to overturn a 3-1 first leg deficit against Always Ready in their home leg as they were held to a goalless draw.

    Real Potosi had finished the match down to 10 men after Kevin Villegas was sent off in stoppage time for violent conduct.

    Players had surrounded Aleman following the final whistle to contest refereeing decisions during the match, with the official then appearing to strike out at Real Potosi goalkeeper Christian Martinez.

    According to Marca, the referee then highlighted a further four red cards to players and dismissed a further three members of Real Potosi's coaching staff.

    Bolivian referee Jordy Aleman was surrounded by Real Potosi players after the Bolivian Cup final. Source: ESPN.

    Footage revealed Aleman lashing out at Real Potosi goalkeeper Christian Martinez amid the confrontation. Source: ESPN.

    It has been revealed that martinez later admitted to insulting the referee, who was surrounded by security after the incident. Source: ESPN.

    Footage then demonstrated Aleman surrounded by security in the aftermath of the incident.

    Martinez later revealed that he had told the official to 'go to hell' and that he 'hoped his mother dies', leading to the referee striking out at him.

    The Argentine goalkeeper noted he had been left with a bloodied mouth following the punch.

    Martinez later issued a statement on social media to confirm he will not pursue legal action or make a complaint about the official following the extraordinary incident.

    'After what happened at the end of the second leg of the Paceña Cup final against Always Ready, where I was punched by referee Jordy Alemán Peralta, I have decided not to initiate legal action or file complaints with the sports authorities,' Martinez wrote on social media.

    'My intention is to put this episode behind me and prevent this situation from continuing to generate conflicts, while remaining fully available to the competent authorities for any clarification that may be necessary.

    'Nothing should overshadow the extraordinary season we've had,.

    'We competed until the very last minute and gave everything on the field for this jersey.'.

    The Bolivian Football Federation are yet to confirm the sanction Aleman will receive following the incident.

    The organisation's disciplinary rules give them the power to impose a ban of up to three years, as well as a fine equivalent to 20 times the national minimum wage.

    #164036. Rembrandt's 'The Night Watch' is more alive than you'd expect

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (946 w)

    Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

    Rembrandt's 'The Night Watch' is more alive than you'd expect

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (946 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, rembrandt van Rijn's "The Night Watch" is one of the most famous paintings of the Dutch Golden Age.
    • In the painting, Rembrandt made dramatic use of light and shadow to guide the viewer's eye to key figures.
    • Beyond the sense of movement featured in "The Night Watch," the painting itself is also alive in a way that's rarely taken into consideration — through the microscopic organisms living on the canvas.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, rembrandt van Rijn's "The Night Watch" is one of the most famous paintings of the Dutch Golden Age. Amsterdam's Rijksmuseum, where the work is on display, hails the artist's 1642 masterpiece as "the turning point in his career and as the superlative example of his creative genius.".

    In the painting, Rembrandt made dramatic use of light and shadow to guide the viewer's eye to key figures. And unlike static group portraits typical of his era, the artist depicted Amsterdam's civic guards in mid-action, as they prepare to march out.

    Beyond the sense of movement featured in "The Night Watch," the painting itself is also alive in a way that's rarely taken into consideration — through the microscopic organisms living on the canvas.

    The research project "The Night Watch Lives" explores exactly that question: What kinds of life forms inhabit the surface of the famous painting?

    The study is a collaborative scientific and exhibition project between the Rijksmuseum and ARTIS-Micropia — an Amsterdam museum dedicated to the world of microorganisms.

    It's part of the broader "Operation Night Watch" restoration and research project described as the "biggest and most wide-ranging ever study and restoration of Rembrandt's most famous painting," started in 2019. Conservators and scientists in this project have been examining every aspect of Rembrandt's masterpiece using cutting-edge technology, seeking upcoming insights into its materials, condition and history — and now, its microbiome.

    It has been revealed that the idea behind "The Night Watch Lives" was to "put microbes in a positive spotlight," Eline van Bloois, who led the research, told DW. "Honestly, if you're asking me — I'm a microbiologist, so I'm biased of course — but they really deserve more positive attention.".

    Over a period of six months, van Bloois will be taking samples once a month directly from the famous painting at the Rijksmuseum, accompanied by the people working on the restoration of "The Night Watch.".

    Using small sterile discs gently pressed against selected areas of the painting, the samples collect microscopic material from both varnished and unvarnished sections.

    These samples are then cultivated in laboratories, allowing previously invisible microbes to grow into visible colonies that can be studied and identified.

    Industry observers note that at the "The Night Watch Lives" exhibition, visitors can view Petri dishes containing the cultivated microbial colonies. A life-size reproduction of Rembrandt's masterpiece also indicates where the samples were taken, and which microorganisms were found there.

    Industry observers note that at the exhibition's opening on November 11, the installation included the findings of two of van Bloois' sampling sessions. Four more will be added over the coming months, allowing the museum's visitors to follow the results of the study as it unfolds.

    That means the exhibition's visitors "will be figuring out what I've found as I'm figuring it out myself," explains the microbiologist. "We really take them through that journey with us.".

    People often fear microbes or associate them with disease, even though the vast majority of these microscopic organisms are actually harmless or vital to human survival.

    Some of the organisms found on the painting "are very commonly found on human skin, for instance, and they're a healthy part of the microbiome; most humans actually have these bacteria with them," notes van Bloois, adding that the presence of these microbes on the painting made sense, since humans are often near the work.

    But another bacterium stood out in the samples: Microbacterium saccharophilum, a species first identified at a sugar refinery in Japan in 2013. How this microorganism ended up on the Dutch "Night Watch," or when, is a guessing game.

    Sources indicate that "It's part of the fun and part of the frustration in microbiology. You cannot ask the microbes where they originate from," states van Bloois. "It would make our lives a bit easier, but it's also fun to have a little bit of a mystery.".

    Recent findings suggest that the samples also revealed bacteria from soil, often found in plant roots. Could these organisms somehow harm the painting? Could plants start growing on the work?

    Van Bloois explains why this is highly unlikely: On the painting, the bacteria can form inactive spores, but for the study, the researcher "provided them with all the nutrients and the right temperature and the right humidity that allowed them to grow again.".

    Still, studying these organisms may eventually contribute to understanding how paintings age, how environmental conditions affect cultural heritage, and how museums can better preserve priceless works of art.

    As to whether the microorganisms could date back to Rembrandt's time, the microbiologist says that's also "highly unlikely" — but here again, microbes cannot reveal their origin story.

    As part of the larger "Operation Night Watch" team, van Bloois is definitely inspired by this "group effort where everyone is just really enthusiastic about telling these stories and adding to the knowledge surrounding 'The Night Watch.'".

    The microbiological samples revealed by the laboratory process resemble abstract art in miniature: colorful clusters, delicate textures and intricate patterns created by living organisms.

    And as the study is unfolding publicly, it also feels like an artistic performance of its own.

    The project also perfectly embodies the full name of the museum where the exhibition is held: Natura Artis Magistra, a Latin phrase that translates to "nature is the teacher of art and science," as the microbiologist points out: "It's really cool to see science and art all come together in this project.".

    The exhibition "The Night Watch Lives" runs at ARTIS-Micropia in Amsterdam until the end of May 2027.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Never be the man after ‘the man’, the saying goes.
    • Recent findings suggest that manchester City have stumbled through a bruising autumn under Enzo Maresca, uncharacteristically so.
    • For a decade, Pep Guardiola bent English football to his will, turning Man City into a relentless, trophy-winning machine.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Never be the man after ‘the man’, the saying goes. Football history is stippled with cautionary tales of managers who followed an all-time great, only to discover that they were doomed from the very beginning.

    Recent findings suggest that manchester City have stumbled through a bruising autumn under Enzo Maresca, uncharacteristically so. It is impossible not to wonder if the Etihad Stadium is experiencing its very own version of Manchester United's 2013/14.

    For a decade, Pep Guardiola bent English football to his will, turning Man City into a relentless, trophy-winning machine. Succeeding a figure who loomed so large over the east side of Manchester was never going to be straightforward. Few, though, expected the drop-off to feel quite so jarring, or quite so familiar.

    It has been revealed that david Moyes arrived at Old Trafford in 2013 tasked with prolonging Sir Alex Ferguson’s dynasty, meanwhile Maresca was handed a three-year contract this summer to keep Guardiola’s juggernaut in motion. Four months into the job, the steering wheel is juddering uncomfortably.

    In a recent development, man City’s recent results make for grim reading compared to the standards set over the last 10 years. A 3-1 defeat away at Nottingham Forest earlier this month was double-take worthy, before Saturday’s 1-1 home draw with Fulham - rescued only by an Elliot Anderson volley - saw them lose yet more ground in the Premier League title race.

    On Tuesday night in the Champions League, Man City needed an 86th-minute Rayan Cherki strike just to salvage a 2-2 draw at home to Napoli, presently eighth in Serie A and 14 points off the pace.

    Ahead of Sunday’s trip to league leaders Arsenal, Maresca's men look a shadow of the team that so recently struck fear into the Gunners' title hopes.

    The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

    Predictably, the question of Maresca’s future has already begun to take on more of a 'when rather than if' feel. Reports emerged this week suggesting the Italian is fighting to save his job barely a third of the way into his debut Etihad campaign. Sack talk at Manchester City circulating at all, never mind in November, speaks volumes about how rapidly things have changed.

    Industry observers note that there are parallels between Man City’s recent slump and Moyes’ 10-month spell across town, too. Like Moyes, Maresca inherited a squad undergoing significant churn after an era of dominance.

    To bridge that gap, City made a throng of big summer purchases, bringing in additions such as Elliot Anderson, Enzo Fernandez, Iliman Ndiaye and Ayyoub Bouaddi.

    Much like Moyes’ integration of Marouane Fellaini and Juan Mata into a fading champion side, Maresca’s new-look Man City feels disjointed - caught between Guardiola’s positional automatisms and a new manager’s attempt to stamp his own authority on the dressing room.

    In a recent development, that disconnect quickly becomes apparent when the team aren't getting results, breeding doubt among players accustomed to certainty and success. All of which begs the question: was Maresca always doomed to fail?

    Following Guardiola was always going to be an exercise in managing impossible expectations while rebuilding in real time. Perhaps the Etihad hierarchy believed their structure would insulate Guardiola’s successor from the same sort of post-Ferguson collapse that swallowed Moyes' efforts - which in hindsight weren't all that bad. Perhaps there is a lesson there for Man City chiefs to heed.

    #164031. Breaking: One of football's most-hyped 16-year-olds - what next for JJ Gabriel?

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1370 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Co ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: One of football's most-hyped 16-year-olds - what next for JJ Gabriel?

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1370 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • JJ Gabriel featured for Manchester United's senior team in pre-season.
    • It has been one of the biggest transfer sagas of the year - around a player who has never played competitive football.
    • Forward JJ Gabriel, who has recently turned 16, walked out on Manchester United in September and now has a verbal agreement to join Real Madrid.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    JJ Gabriel featured for Manchester United's senior team in pre-season.

    It has been one of the biggest transfer sagas of the year - around a player who has never played competitive football.

    Forward JJ Gabriel, who has recently turned 16, walked out on Manchester United in September and now has a verbal agreement to join Real Madrid.

    Before even playing a senior game - barring friendlies - he has told Spanish newspaper Marca his "dream is to win the Ballon d'Or".

    Gabriel's real name is Joseph Junior Andreou O'Cearuill - with Cypriot and Irish lineage - but he changed his name, reportedly for commercial purposes.

    Recent findings suggest that his father, London-born Joe O'Cearuill, played twice for the Republic of Ireland - but the highest level he played at club level was a loan spell with Brighton in League One and one minute in the Uefa Cup with St Patrick's Athletic. He has been actively involved in his son's career.

    Gabriel was scheduled to become Manchester United's youngest ever player in the Carabao Cup against Brighton on 16 September, but had told the club he planned to leave by then.

    In a recent development, how long will Gabriel have to wait for a first-team debut now? In the past 10 years Real have only handed two debuts to 17-year-olds and none to a 16-year-old.

    When Real boss Jose Mourinho was asked about Gabriel on Friday, he said: "I don't have a feeling [about Gabriel]. I don't have a feeling with players who don't work with me.".

    In fact, Real have not even announced anything yet - despite Gabriel posting a 50-second video montage on social media saying goodbye to United this week.

    Madrid-bound Gabriel posts farewell Man Utd message.

    Why schoolboys have become a huge part of football's transfer market.

    For a while now Madrid have been getting the best young talents early and turning them into Galacticos before they cost in excess of 100m euros.

    Vinicius Junior and Rodrygo came that way, then Endrick - and Gabriel is seen as the next.

    It has been revealed that it fits the policy run by Jose Angel Sanchez, the director general, and Juni Calafat, head of scouting. It is a long-term bet on one of the most promising young players in the international game.

    According to recent reports, barcelona looked at him too, and backed away because the commissions were too high. Madrid believe in the player so much that they were willing to pay whatever it took to get the deal done.

    Sources indicate that the expectations are very high and the aim is for him to reach the first team. They want him at Castilla - Real's reserve team - but the situation right now does not allow it.

    Castilla and Real Madrid C cannot sign players until January, so for the time being he is expected to play for the Juvenil - the under-18s.

    Madrid also learned from the Martin Odegaard period that training with the first team while playing for the B side is a bad idea. So the plan is a spell in the B side, and when he is ready, Gabriel jumps straight into the first team.

    Recent findings suggest that where Madrid are less happy is with how things have unfolded. Madrid wanted to set the timing themselves and be discreet, because they do not want problems with Manchester United and do not want to upset anyone. At Real Madrid, nobody is bigger than the club.

    Industry observers note that the idea was to keep everything quiet until January and announce it then. But with Gabriel already training in Madrid, the secret was never going to last.

    Who is Gabriel's newly introduced agent, Ali Barat?

    "Players are moving to him because his reputation is that he'll get you a move to a bigger club," one Premier League club source told BBC Sport.

    Dubai-based Barat does not just consider himself a super-agent, but a "boutique" super-agent.

    Born in Iran and raised in London, Barat says he fell into football almost by accident after many years in international business.

    After initially working as an intermediary at low-level clubs, he founded Epic Sports in January 2020.

    His major football experience before that? The football game Championship Manager.

    Sources indicate that "I was always trading players," he told ESPN this year. "I was obsessed with every single player around the world.".

    In a recent development, this was not just about living out a fantasy in the real world. Barat was drawn into the profession because of the vast sums agents can earn in commission.

    Sources indicate that what makes his agency "boutique"? Unlike the top operations which have a huge number of players on their books, Epic Sports aims to have just 22 - two for each position.

    This, Barat argues, ensures there is never any conflict of interest in how he represents his players.

    Barat offers bespoke management of a player's career and came to prominence in the summer of 2025 when 15 of his players moved on.

    Recent findings suggest that this included Dean Huijsen joining Real Madrid, Nicolas Jackson moving to Bayern Munich and Xavi Simons signing for Tottenham Hotspur. Noni Madueke left Chelsea for Arsenal, and the Gunners signed Piero Hincapie.

    This led to Barat being named Golden Boy Best Agent for the second time in three years.

    Yet he is largely the figurehead, with agents working on his behalf around Europe. For instance, Epic has three other agents registered with the English Football Association (FA).

    Barat, who also brokered Moises Caicedo's move to Chelsea, claims he uses social media, and in particular influencer Fabrizio Romano, to amplify stories and agree transfers on his terms.

    He is an unashamed self-publicist, too.

    Industry observers note that "Ali Barat redefines the game again," read an Epic Sports press release to announce Jackson's loan move to Bayern. No other agency seems to promote itself in this way.

    The largely AI-generated video which announced Gabriel had joined Epic Sports was right on brand.

    Gabriel's deal is part of a fresh venture: Epic Future - and this presents an ethical problem.

    Sources indicate that "It is about targeting the biggest young players, especially where they're not necessarily on the longest contracts," a Premier League source said. "And move them overseas for cheap fees.

    "The original club will get a few 100,000 euros if that, and everyone else will hoover up millions and millions and millions - including his family.".

    Transferring a player to Europe also opens the door to future sell-on fees for an agent, which is against FA regulations.

    It is this upcoming focus on younger players which has started to cause friction at some top clubs.

    No club wants to lose players they have spent years developing for nothing, only for an agent to reap the rewards.

    Manchester United had to work hard 18 months ago to convince JJ Gabriel and his family that Old Trafford was the right place to further his football education.

    The significant question is, did they overpromise in doing so?

    Sources close to the player eventually felt they were let down and United did not deliver on what was expected.

    Certainly around Gabriel's pre-season minutes and presence in the squad for the Champions League opener against Azerbaijan title winners Sabah FK, which it was felt would be a perfect opportunity for the youngster to make his debut.

    By the time the Carabao Cup tie against Brighton came round, there was no faith Gabriel would be brought on. Given United lost 3-2, there is merit in that stance.

    The secondary elements are where will Gabriel develop the most?

    United's academy is one of the best in England at producing young players, but given his size, will the forward benefit more from being in a less physical environment?

    There has been a lot of sniping around his decision to leave United, but his stats are impressive and he is clearly a player of huge potential. United would certainly have wished the situation had not unfolded the way it has.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Arsenal could lose a first-team defender who has fallen out of favour with manager Mikel Arteta.

    The Gunners boast arguably the best backline in Europe at the moment, having conceded the fewest goals in the Premier League this term (just seven), and goalkeeper David Raya has already kept seven clean sheets in 11 fixtures.

    Part of Arsenal's strength at the back is in their depth – but that could be seriously impacted with interest in a star who hasn't been getting in the team as much of late.

    Following a back injury at the 2026 World Cup to William Saliba, the Gunners moved to bring in quality cover in the shape of England international Ezri Konsa.

    Konsa has been an instant hit at the Emirates Stadium, and with Arteta now boasting eight senior players competing for places – Konsa, Saliba, Gabriel and Cristhian Mosquera in the centre, with full-backs Jurrien Timber, Ben White, Riccardo Calafiori and Piero Hincapie all capable in the middle, too – the problem is giving each of them playing time.

    Sport Witness have now relayed a report from L’Interista that claims Inter Milan are interested in Mosquera, who started the Gunners' first three games of the season in all competitions but hasn't featured much of late.

    The Spaniard filled in for Saliba before the Konsa deal was completed, but went off injured against Aston Villa in the second league game of the campaign, paving the way for Konsa to make his debut.

    The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

    The 29-year-old has kept his place alongside Gabriel ever since – and despite Saliba returning to fitness and featuring on the bench recently, the former Villa star has remained a mainstay of the team.

    This has left Mosquera out in the cold as the fourth-choice, and though the ex-Valencia man can play across the backline, White and Timber have rotated for the right-back slot, while Calafiori and Hincapie have shared left-back, leaving him with very few minutes since the start of the campaign.

    Mosquera only signed last summer, but with ESPN reporting the transfer fee to be just £13 million, Arsenal may well consider flipping the 22-year-old for a steep profit, with the report claiming Arsenal want around £30m for his signature.

    The champions also have a homegrown talent in the form of Marli Salmon, still just 17 years old but having already impressed both centrally and at right-back.

    FourFourTwo understands that Arsenal have no interest in selling Mosquera in January but could reassess the situation next summer.

    Mosquera is worth €40 million, according to Transfermarkt. Arsenal host Manchester City this weekend when Premier League action resumes.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Manchester United strategy to address their issues at left-back by signing a player dubbed ‘the next Riccardo Calafiori’, following another poor result away at Sporting.

    The Red Devils dropped two points in Europe last night away in Lisbon, with latest manager Mauricio Pochettino winless in his first two games in charge, as the scale of the task at hand becomes clear.

    With Manchester United 19th in both the Premier League and the Champions League's league phase right now, Pochettino is under pressure to deliver promptly, with January earmarked for much-needed newly introduced signings.

    Once again, United have struggled at left-back this season, with veteran Luke Shaw injured for much of the campaign.

    Lisandro Martinez started the 4-0 defeat to Liverpool in Pochettino's first fixture, while Diogo Dalot has played out of position to cover there this term, with no obvious candidate to step in during Shaw's absence.

    Sport Witness, however, have relayed a report from Gazzetta dello Sport, which claims that United have “already made moves” to sign Juan Miranda of Bologna.

    The Spaniard signed for I Rossoblu following the sale of Riccardo Calafiori to Arsenal, and has impressed in Serie A with similar attacking instincts and reliable performances in manager Raffaele Palladino's backline.

    The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

    While Bologna are looking to tie Miranda down until 2030, there is significant interest from both Pochettino and Newcastle United, who see the 26-year-old as an option to alleviate the burden on Lewis Hall at left-back.

    FourFourTwo understands that the Red Devils have a modest budget for January and may be limited in what they can do in the transfer market – meaning that cost-effective signings like Miranda may be the way forward, should Pochettino wish to strengthen.

    After finishing third in the Premier League last season, manager Michael Carrick welcomed four fresh faces to Carrington in the form of Andrey Santos, Carlos Baleba, Youri Tielemans – all midfielders – and backup goalkeeper Karl Darlow, along with the returning Marcus Rashford, following his successful stint on loan with Barcelona.

    While the lack of depth in defence and attack has been obvious this season though, United's midfield acquisitions have been questioned too for their lack of dynamism, with Carrick ultimately paying for the side's atrocious form with his job after just 10 league games.

    United have won just three matches all season in all competitions.

    Miranda is worth €15 million, according to Transfermarkt. Manchester United face Brentford this weekend when Premier League action resumes.

    Breaking: Defending in the Premier League has changed – and it’s causing chaos

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1149 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later?
    • As Ronald Araujo prepared to play a long ball forward and Leny Yoro stood close to the halfway line, alarm bells were ringing in the heads of several former Premier League defenders.
    • Everything about Yoro’s positioning and response to Araujo sending the pass over the top went against what those former players would recognise as the principles of playing next to a centre-back partner, the rules of playing in a back four that have been passed down for generations.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

    As Ronald Araujo prepared to play a long ball forward and Leny Yoro stood close to the halfway line, alarm bells were ringing in the heads of several former Premier League defenders.

    Everything about Yoro’s positioning and response to Araujo sending the pass over the top went against what those former players would recognise as the principles of playing next to a centre-back partner, the rules of playing in a back four that have been passed down for generations.

    Yoro did not begin to drop when it became clear that Araujo was going long. He did not anticipate the threat of danger by providing cover for Matthijs De Ligt, as he and Alexander Isak challenged for the ball. Instead, Yoro watched on, as if it was not his responsibility.

    By the time he had reacted to De Ligt’s mistake, it was already far too late; in chasing Isak down and crashing into the striker outside of the box, he left Manchester United down to 10 men for the majority of their 4-0 defeat to Liverpool at Anfield in Mauricio Pochettino’s first match in charge (the Frenchman’s one-match ban was subsequently overturned after United won their appeal for wrongful dismissal).

    Yoro, though, had only followed the instructions Pochettino and his coaching staff had issued him. The 21-year-old wasn’t even playing as a centre-back partner for De Ligt, as such; with United instead looking to defend Liverpool man-for-man, it was, in a sense, every man for himself. Yoro appeared more concerned with Florian Wirtz, the Liverpool creator who was positioned 15 yards away, than covering Isak with De Ligt. He was, effectively, tasked with thinking as a defensive midfielder as well as a centre-back.

    To measure just how the responsibilities of the Premier League centre-back have changed, take how Gary Neville spent the closing stages of United’s defeat during his commentary for Sky Sports describing the lessons he learned in his formative years. As a youth, Neville was taught how to play in a back four by holding onto a long rope with his fellow defenders. The exercise was designed to build cohesion and form the idea that the pieces of a defensive line were inter-connected, so that when a full-back rushes out wide to close down a winger, the rest of the defence moves with them, or that when one centre-back jumps forward to attack a long ball, the other drops in behind.

    Those commandments are likely to still be repeated across parks and astroturfs as youngsters learn the game today, but it sounds horribly out of date when compared to the very elite, where tactical shifts within the Premier League and top leagues can make modern football appear as a different sport – where bravery and risks are embraced and caution is cut out.

    In a recent development, fulham’s approach at Manchester City on Saturday was another example. Fulham had lost 17 consecutive matches against City in the Premier League and were facing the league’s best striker in Erling Haaland. Did Alvaro Arbeloa’s side look to be safe? To keep it tight and compact to get through the opening stages of a difficult away game? It wasn’t even a consideration.

    Within two minutes, Calvin Bassey could be seen leaving his inexperienced (in Premier League terms) centre-back partner David Affengruber one-on-one with Haaland on the halfway line, as he pushed forward to mark Phil Foden. For Arbeloa’s gameplan to work and Fulham to press City, Bassey had to trust that Affengruber, in his sixth Premier League appearance, could be left to deal with Haaland by himself.

    Recent findings suggest that bassey and Affengruber were individually outstanding as Fulham held City to a 1-1 draw, but then they had to be. There is an argument that playing centre-back for a team that looks to press high and go man-to-man across the pitch is now the hardest position in the sport. It requires defenders to not only win their individual duels against skilful dribblers but cover huge areas of space against fast forwards, often as the last one back. They have to be strong physically, have excellent recovery speed and be dominant aerially, as well as being technically sound and capable of playing line-splitting passes, or else they would be seen as a liability in possession. They have to be seen as leaders, to be commanding, brave, and an effective communicator.

    In a recent development, and there is nowhere to hide if one of those pieces falls through. The decisions and tactical set-up that led to Yoro’s sending off at Anfield was brilliantly covered by Jamie Carragher and former Tottenham centre-back Toby Alderweireld on Sky’s Monday Night Football, but the struggles of Levi Colwill and Wesley Fofana following Chelsea’s 4-1 defeat at home to Leeds was dissected as well. “You feel like you’re watching kids play in a men’s game,” was Carragher’s assessment of Colwill and Fofana. Yet Fofana was a £75m-rated centre-back when he was signed from Leicester at the age of 21 four years ago; Colwill may have gone for a similar fee following his breakthrough season on loan at Roberto De Zerbi’s Brighton three years ago.

    Recent findings suggest that the value of finding a player who can meet the demands of the modern-day centre-back was underlined when Arsenal decided to spend up to £55m on 28-year-old Ezri Konsa, rather than play the first three months of the season without a suitable replacement for the injured William Saliba. Liverpool similarly went substantial on Jeremy Jacquet, spending up to £60m after he had barely played a full season at Rennes. The early impact of the 21-year-old, next to Virgil van Dijk, suggests Liverpool knew what they were getting; the combination of technical quality and athleticism, which has become even more valuable in a high-pressing team under Andoni Iraola.

    Industry observers note that yet one of the reasons Liverpool landed Jacquet was because they missed out on signing Yoro two years before when he was an 18-year-old at Lille. United swooped to pay a reported £52.1m for a player who had entered the final 12 months on his contract, with Real Madrid and Paris Saint-Germain also pursuing a deal. They all saw what United did too: a young centre-back who had all the attributes needed to play as part of a high defensive line and win his duels in one-on-one situations.

    Yoro can still be that player. He is, in many ways, an ideal centre-back for Pochettino, who learned at Anfield that De Ligt, post back injury, is not. Yoro will be available for United against Brentford on Saturday, attempting to rebuild his confidence on the high wire that modern-day centre-backs have to tread.

    Mikel Arteta may prefer to imagine his Arsenal team as a remorseless winning machine, although on nights such as these they can still demonstrate a familiar unreliability when it comes to the main purpose of it all.

    It has been revealed that there were 30 shots over the night from the English champions, only four of which were on target, and in the end their winner never came. Even in the 95th minute, Arteta’s players were still conspiring to foul it up. This Champions League game might have been decided in Arsenal’s favour within 20 minutes. By half-time it should have been a formality. Yet, as chance after chance slipped away, there was always a possibility this would end differently.

    According to recent reports, the leaders of the Bundesliga were traumatised at times by the ferocity of the Arsenal press, and there were times when Borussia Dortmund will likely have no idea how they survived. Even so, they did just that and, liberated in the second half, Maximilian Beier scored an improbable equaliser in his team’s best period. There were still 40 minutes for Arsenal to put this one to bed and they found many ways not to do so.

    It was notable that the man who put Arsenal ahead in the ninth minute with a right-footed thump from space on the edge of the Dortmund box was the same striker who would miss the best chance to win it. That is the Viktor Gyökeres dilemma. In the space of a single game he can look like a potential match-winner and also the last man his manager would wish to see arriving on the end of a perfect Martin Odegaard cross.

    Recent findings suggest that so it proved after 75 minutes when Gyökeres thrust himself at an Odegaard ball into the box that just needed guiding inside a post, yet planted it decisively wide of the mark. On the touchline Arteta tried very hard to hide his despair and failed to do so.

    It ended that way, with a heroic defensive performance from the Dortmund defence, including one memorable moment when substitute Serhou Guirassy’s determination to block a cross prompted a double ricochet off his own post. One could make the argument that there were times when it was “unbelievable”, as Arteta later remarked, that the ball did not find its way in. Although there were also moments when the reasons were self-evident.

    “There’s an element of luck,” the Arsenal manager stated, “and there is an element of us [not] finishing better.”.

    In a recent development, in fifth place in the league phase table, dropped points at home do not carry the same jeopardy in the group stage that they once did, yet even so there was a truth for Arteta to chew upon. This is a well-honed, big-game Arsenal Champions League side that he has built. One that reached the final last season and may well go close again, but as ever they seem to be doing so in spite of the great goalscorer that so many of their nearest rivals have at their disposal.

    Sources indicate that arteta sounded that warning after defeat in the final in Budapest at the end of May and, while changes have been made, it would be hard to argue that they have been fundamental. This was a good opponent – the leaders of the Bundesliga with many exports from English football who have been reconditioned for the German game. Those include Fábio Silva, Felix Nmecha and Jobe Bellingham, who had a second-half goal narrowly disallowed for offside.

    I’m very impressed with them, with what Niko has done with the team, especially the way they are playing, the way they are dominating games, the amount of threat that they are able to create.

    We had them here in pre-season (a 3-2 defeat) and they indicated their quality and what they are capable of, so we are very much aware of that.

    But we play at home in front of our crowd and we’re going to go and attack the game, that’s for sure.

    Mikel Arteta seems quite set on his left-back pecking order: Riccardo Calafiori starts on weekends, and Piero Hincapie starts in midweek. They are very different players (Calafiori is the more adventurous, while Hincapie is more of an old-school defender) and it seems that Arteta feels Hincapie is better suited to Champions League football. He’ll be tested tonight against the Bundesliga leaders.

    Industry observers note that by Yannick HuberOn Tuesday, all eyes will be on Ethan Nwaneri. The Champions League clash between Arsenal and Borussia Dortmund marks the 19-year-old’s return to the club where he grew up, where he became the Premier League’s youngest player and from whom he joined Dortmund on loan in the summer. It would be hard to imagine a more poignant setting. But for Nwaneri, facing Arsenal is about more than a reunion. It is also an opportunity to finally make his mark at Dortmund.

    Sources indicate that so far his time in Germany has not gone according to plan. Nwaneri arrived with a considerable reputation and high expectations, but has become less prominent in recent weeks. His playing time has diminished and he has frequently had to settle for a place on the bench.

    But there are several reasons to believe that, of all games, this meeting with his former club could give his Dortmund career fresh impetus.

    Arsenal: Kepa; White, Konsa, Gabriel, Hincapie; Rice, Lewis-Skelly; Madueke, Odegaard, Tzolis; GyokeresSubs: Meslier, Porter, Saliba, Mosquera, Eze, Timber, Merino, Havertz, Calafiori, Guimaraes, Dowman.

    Dortmund: Kobel, Ryerson, Anton, Schlotterbeck, Gadou, Svensson, Veerman, Nmecha, Bellingham, Beier, SilvaSubs: Drewes, Meyer, Bensebaini, Guirassy, Chukwuemeka, Nwaneri, Karetsas, Sabitzer, Mane, Albert, Dos Santos, Reggiani.

    Mikel Arteta was an Arsenal player the last time they played Borussia Dortmund in the Champions League, and tonight he will have to make do without first-choice goalkeeper David Raya.

    Arsenal’s manager struck an upbeat note when describing the shoulder or upper arm injury Raya sustained at Newcastle, and it appears he has avoided a long-term absence.

    Even two weeks out, however, would mean Raya missing Premier League fixtures against Manchester City, Brentford and Spurs – possibly Arsenal’s most testing week of the season. Arteta did not rule out a return to face City on Sunday.

    In a recent development, kepa Arrizabalaga is expected to deputise against Dortmund, who are top of the Bundesliga and have won three of their four Champions League league phase games. They won at the Emirates in a pre-season friendly, and Jobe Bellingham and on-loan Arsenal attacker Ethan Nwaneri are among their ranks.

    These Champions League fixtures can feel secondary in importance to Premier League fare because of the competition’s fresh format, but a top-two finish in the league phase is a serious incentive.

    As Arsenal discovered to their benefit last season when they “won” the league phase, the top two teams are rewarded with home second legs all the way to the final.

    Arsenal are at the moment third on 10 points and face Real Madrid at the Emirates next, the team above them in second, so victory this evening is essential to set up that occasion.

    Arteta has tended to make between four and six changes for these games, and Ben White, Piero Hincapie, Myles Lewis-Skelly, Christos Tzolis and Viktor Gyokeres are players pushing for starts after starting on the bench at Newcastle.

    Also among the substitutes at St James’ Park was William Saliba, who is stepping up his return from a long-term back injury and could play his first minutes of the season tonight.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Is there a better central midfielder on the planet than Jude Bellingham right now?
    • Recent findings suggest that not according to Jose Mourinho.
    • "He has physicality, he has technique, he has tactical understanding of the game, he has ambition, he has absolutely everything," Mourinho said.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Bellingham finished 11th in the 2026 Ballon d'Or.

    Is there a better central midfielder on the planet than Jude Bellingham right now?

    Recent findings suggest that not according to Jose Mourinho. The Real Madrid manager might be trying to manage the Englishman's minutes, but he did not hold back in his praise after the 23-year-old came off the bench and scored a superb volley, helping Real overturn a half-time deficit to beat PSV Eindhoven 5-1.

    "He has physicality, he has technique, he has tactical understanding of the game, he has ambition, he has absolutely everything," Mourinho said.

    "He's an absolutely extraordinary player and for me, without any doubt, the best midfielder in the world.".

    Bellingham's impressive 45-minute cameo came just nine days after an outstanding, all-action display for England in a 3-2 Nations League win in Spain.

    While the former Birmingham and Borussia Dortmund player also earned plenty of plaudits for his displays at the 2026 World Cup, where he scored seven times, Mourinho believes Bellingham's unique blend of craft and graft isn't yet fully appreciated.

    According to recent reports, "He can play as a '10', as an '8', with two pivots, with one," Mourinho said after the win against PSV. "That's why I said, when the Ballon d'Or was discussed, that it was outrageous he wasn't among the top 10.".

    While wingers like Lamine Yamal or Michael Olise are also likely to be contenders for the 2027 award, is there anyone you would rather have in central midfield than Bellingham?

    BBC Sport looks at what makes him so good, and who his closest challengers are.

    Is Bellingham presently 'the best player in the world'?

    Although only 23, Bellingham is already in his fourth year at Real Madrid and is on course for his most productive campaign since his debut season in 2023-24, when he scored 23 goals and provided 13 assists, including setting up Vinicius Jr in the Champions League final.

    Recent findings suggest that he has seven goals and four assists in 18 appearances this season. Only three central midfielders have more goal involvements across Europe's top five leagues, but Bellingham's all-round game is what sets him apart.

    He leads his Real team-mates for possession won, duels won and fouls won. And while only Kylian Mbappe has had more shots on target, Bellingham offers far more than just late runs into the box.

    He has played more passes into the final third than any other Real player, leads the club for ball carries and is second only to Arda Guler for chances created.

    When Bellingham's coaches at Birmingham gave him the number 22 shirt, it reflected their belief that he could play any role, as a number 10, 8 or 4.

    He has fulfilled that potential to become the complete midfielder.

    While Bellingham made his senior debut with Birmingham, Vitinha also spent part of his formative years in the Midlands, scoring once in 22 appearances during a loan spell at Wolves - a spectacular long-range strike against Chorley in 2021.

    But goalscoring isn't what the Portuguese playmaker is best known for - it is his metronomic passing.

    The 26-year-old has played a pivotal role in Paris St-Germain's back-to-back Champions League triumphs, with manager Luis Enrique saying he "embodies the perfect midfielder".

    He was named man of the match in the victory over Arsenal last season, having completed 141 of his 150 passes, matching the Champions League final record set by Barcelona's Xavi in 2011.

    Vitinha finished third in the Ballon d'Or voting in 2025 but slipped to 14th this year, a ranking Luis Enrique disagreed with.

    Recent findings suggest that "It's a real pleasure to have a player with such physical abilities and that mentality," the PSG boss noted last month. "He's at an incredible level.".

    Rice finished one place below Vitinha, and four below England team-mate Bellingham, in the 2026 Ballon d'Or rankings after helping Arsenal win their first Premier League title since 2004.

    According to recent reports, he briefly played at centre-back as a youngster at West Ham before establishing himself as a top-class defensive midfielder for the Hammers. But since joining the Gunners in 2023 he has taken his game to another level, adding significantly more attacking output.

    Rice created 17 big chances in the Premier League last season, as defined by Opta, a total bettered only by Bruno Fernandes and Rayan Cherki.

    The 27-year-old has also registered 14 assists in all club competitions since August 2025. While set-pieces have undoubtedly contributed to that tally, he offers much more.

    He ranks among the top 4% of central midfielders across Europe's top five leagues for progressive carries, while posting similarly impressive figures for chances created, touches and expected assists.

    The 2024 Ballon d'Or winner missed Spain's Nations League defeat by England this month through injury, and his absence was keenly felt as the hosts uncharacteristically struggled for control, at least against 11 men.

    It was a far cry from Spain's triumphant Euro 2024 and 2026 World Cup campaigns, both of which ended with him being named player of the tournament.

    The 30-year-old completed 756 passes as Spain won their second global title, the highest total ever recorded at a World Cup.

    His performances this summer were all the more impressive given that he had taken time to return to his best after tearing his anterior cruciate ligament, an injury that sidelined him for most of the 2024-25 campaign.

    The former Manchester City player has slotted in seamlessly since joining Barcelona in August, and averages 106 successful passes per 90 minutes in La Liga - the second-highest figure, behind Vitinha, of any player in the top five European leagues.

    The student playing in La Liga: Introvert Rodri's unique rise to top.

    Pedri may be six years younger than Rodri, his midfield partner at the Camp Nou, but he boasts extraordinary experience for a 24-year-old, having made more than 250 appearances for Barcelona, not to mention playing at two European Championships and two World Cups.

    The Tenerife-born midfielder combines tigerish work-rate with quality in possession.

    He has created 26 chances from open play in La Liga this season, the sixth-highest total across Europe's top five leagues, and wins possession an average of 7.6 times per 90 minutes, the 10th-highest figure.

    However, such is Spain's wealth of midfield options that he is not even guaranteed a starting place for his country, with Fabian Ruiz preferred for their final three matches at the 2026 World Cup.

    Paris St-Germain midfielder Ruiz, who finished 10th in this year's Ballon d'Or rankings, also deserves to be in any debate about the world's best midfielders.

    He might not yet have the profile of Barcelona team-mates Rodri or Pedri, but on current form alone, versatile youngster Lopez is one of Europe's best box-to-box goalscorers.

    The 23-year-old already has nine goals and seven assists this season. Counting only goals scored in Europe's top five leagues and the Champions League, no central midfielder has more.

    While Lopez can also operate on the wing, the presence of Lamine Yamal and Anthony Gordon means he has mainly featured as a number eight or a number 10 this term.

    The Barcelona academy graduate played only a bit-part role as Spain won Euro 2024 and was unfortunate to miss the World Cup after breaking a bone in his foot in May.

    However, a summer off enabled him to hit the ground running this season, and he has not looked back.

    “I wondered if there might be a problem”: Schwarzer on Venables at Boro

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Mark Schwarzer has revealed that he feared a difficult reunion with Terry Venables when the former Australia manager arrived at Middlesbrough – only to find that the coach was willing to put their past disagreement behind them.
    • The pair had fallen out over Schwarzer’s availability for international duty in 1997, when the goalkeeper chose to honour a commitment to Boro rather than join an Australia squad under Venables.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Mark Schwarzer has revealed that he feared a difficult reunion with Terry Venables when the former Australia manager arrived at Middlesbrough – only to find that the coach was willing to put their past disagreement behind them.

    The pair had fallen out over Schwarzer’s availability for international duty in 1997, when the goalkeeper chose to honour a commitment to Boro rather than join an Australia squad under Venables.

    Schwarzer had reason to worry about the potential for awkwardness when Venables was appointed to work alongside Bryan Robson at the Riverside in December 2000, tasked with helping Middlesbrough to beat the drop.

    Schwarzer told FourFourTwo: “I was worried when Terry came in, because his previous job had been manager of Australia.

    “I’d just joined Middlesbrough when we had that League Cup semi-final at the same time as an Australia call-up.

    "Terry had made it clear that if he called you up, he expected you to be there.

    "Bryan Robson asked him if I could stay because it was one of the biggest games in Middlesbrough’s history.”.

    The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

    In a recent development, “Terry initially agreed, then three days beforehand called and mentioned I had to choose. I told him I’d made a commitment to my club. He didn’t pick me again, including for the World Cup play-off against Iran.

    Industry observers note that “When he arrived at Middlesbrough, I wondered if there might be a problem. To his credit, he was brilliant. He basically said 'These things happen, let’s move on'.".

    Instead of allowing the dispute to linger, Schwarzer says Venables did a fantastic job of working out how to get Middlesbrough back in form.

    It has been revealed that he said: “He made a huge impact at Middlesbrough. He spoke to everyone about what they thought was going wrong, then made his own mind up about how to address it.

    It has been revealed that “Terry was exceptional at not undermining Bryan. Robbo was still at the front of things but had this incredible coach to learn from. If Terry hadn’t come in, we would have been relegated.”.

    Boro eventually finished the 2000-01 Premier League season in 14th, well clear of the drop.

    #164017. Inside the mind games that will decide Arsenal v Man City

    📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1361 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Co ↗ Open Full Page

    Inside the mind games that will decide Arsenal v Man City

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1361 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later?
    • Manchester City have a lot of bigger concerns right now but some of Enzo Maresca’s staff have naturally been conscious of the noise around David Raya.
    • It’s certainly true the injury suffered at Newcastle United is nowhere near as bad as first feared, with contact on a nerve having apparently caused the initial glitch.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

    Manchester City have a lot of bigger concerns right now but some of Enzo Maresca’s staff have naturally been conscious of the noise around David Raya. The goalkeeper was not wearing a sling at Tuesday’s Champions League match against Borussia Dortmund, after he had so conspicuously been photographed sporting one on London’s busiest street just two days before.

    It’s certainly true the injury suffered at Newcastle United is nowhere near as bad as first feared, with contact on a nerve having apparently caused the initial glitch.

    Recent findings suggest that some on the City side have wondered whether Mikel Arteta is using it to play his usual games. The manager likes to use media and even official squad photos to keep opposition guessing.

    It would be especially understandable here, since this position could go a long way to deciding Sunday’s game.

    The entire decision on Raya, in fact, draws out so many of its strands and storylines.

    Both sides are especially attuned to it since it was as recently as March's Carabao Cup final that Pep Guardiola’s response to the Kepa Arrizabalaga selection essentially decided that game.

    It might even have been the Catalan’s last piece of genius in England. Arsenal couldn’t play out of the press without Raya's passing, and City gradually shut them down. The tactical effect of it was so pronounced that it framed the thinking of both clubs ahead of April’s suffocatingly tense Premier League showdown.

    According to recent reports, that 2-1 City win might well go down as one of those influential defeats, rather than decisive victories, because of the effect on Arsenal. They actually gleaned confidence and instruction, to win all of their remaining games.

    And now they're champions, and intent on asserting exactly what that means - with Raya's injury right now the primary concern.

    In a recent development, except, aside from it looking 50-50 over whether Raya will be involved, Guardiola certainly won’t be. The man responsible for that tactical thinking isn't there. And even if there is now debate over Maresca’s exact quality as a coach, he’s not Guardiola.

    The dysfunction of his own pressing system, and City’s newly profound susceptibility to counter-attacks, also means they may not be able to execute any such approach in the same way… but then very little about City is the same.

    The very consequence of this match might even change.

    It all adds to the feel of this being a defining game for this most peculiar of seasons.

    Arsenal can win to emphatically kill City’s title challenge… but will that even be a title challenge? City can win to transform the entire dynamic around the top of the table, but will the outcome of their appeal skew it in a way the Premier League has never seen?

    Or, what if they win and then win their appeal - however unlikely legal figures right now think that is - to then go on a run?

    It’s an absurd context, and that for a fixture that has recently been freighted with greater meaning.

    And it is because of that recent history that Arsenal do feel they owe City one.

    Arteta is stated to feel it was absolutely crucial they won the title before Guardiola left and the verdict of the long-running Premier League case came in.

    It has been revealed that it was about proving it on their own terms. And now, with City precarious, they want to fully prove their superiority; to emphasise this can be their era; to put City out of the picture.

    Despite enduring two comebacks for draws in their last two matches, the Arsenal squad are in a good mood.

    They feel they played excellently for 160 minutes of those games and that just continuing that will have them in good stead over an awkward run of fixtures.

    Or, as one figure told the Independent: “We are due to hammer someone”.

    And, as another said separately: “We need to hammer City on Sunday”.

    Everyone at Arsenal knows that is much easier said than done.

    Despite all of City’s recent problems, the rivalry of this fixture might just be the type of game Maresca’s side require. It might cause them to dig deep.

    That of course may depend on how deep their problems actually are.

    One recent argument coming out of City has been that this is all just tactical, and individual moments in individual games are going against them.

    It’s just that the idea this slump is solely down to tactical/technical issues feels… a stretch.

    Really, City are in a situation of remarkable extremes.

    According to recent reports, even the departure of Guardiola would have been enough to distort an entire season. If City are obviously better structured than Manchester United after Sir Alex Ferguson or Arsenal themselves after Arsene Wenger, it is still adapting to the absence of one of the most psychologically imposing figures in football. His presence was immense.

    That alone creates a vacuum, that is arguably manifesting in City's dysfunctional midfield.

    That area also poses significant tactical questions about Guardiola's successor. Insiders familiar with both Chelsea and Leicester City can’t help notice familiar flaws in Maresca’s teams, especially as regards the balance. City are just so easy to get at.

    Sources indicate that you can even map previous Chelsea form onto this season. Maresca’s first season at Stamford Bridge in 2024-25 started well, to the point of being talked of as title challengers, only to endure a winter drop-off surrounded by the same tactical discussions.

    And then, there’s the guilty verdict.

    The City squad are going through a situation no one in English football history has ever experienced. You can even extend that to European football, despite various controversies, given how long this entire process has been.

    Another line from inside the club is that they are as adamant with the players as they are with everyone else: that they will overturn this verdict, and significant questions will instead be posted to the rest of the Premier League.

    Some at rival clubs even think that one element of City’s belligerent response, at least in public, has been as a message to the players.

    Sources indicate that they need to radiate a sense of business as usual so as to convince the squad, because they do need the actual football business to indeed be as it usually is. They know they need to keep them focused.

    That’s just very difficult to do when the potential consequences could come this season, which recent results arguably show.

    Sources indicate that because, even if the players themselves honestly insist they are genuinely fully focused, this is still a story that has major implications for their careers. They may have to take significant decisions. Some might even be thinking this is a waste of a season in a short career.

    That is going to at least have some effect, even if it is subconscious.

    It creates a cloud of doubt, and this in a sport that demands more intensity of focus than ever before. The opposition manager, Arteta, demands it more than anyone else. Guardiola himself was a huge influence in this.

    Both have abruptly discarded numerous players if they sensed that a necessary tunnel vision had been obscured by even 1 per cent.

    According to recent reports, and that is exactly what a situation like this does. It's too massive to just completely shut out.

    Without it, City might have even been better able to work around some of the tactical issues.

    In short, even if performances have been OK, this does not look like a team playing to optimum level.

    Neither do Arsenal but they don’t feel too far off. They're primed. City might well need that challenge to rouse themselves.

    In a recent development, either way, it is already a fixture that feels like it has the makings of a huge result. And also a result that might mean absolutely nothing by the end.
