    Industry News: Budget cuts threaten Germany's fight against antisemitism and racism

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (950 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that initiatives and organizations in Germany are speaking out against planned budget cuts to the work of strengthening democracy and fighting racism and antisemitism.
    • It has been revealed that the "Living democracy" (Demokratie Leben) program from the Ministry for Family Affairs is set to receive a total of €170 million ($187 million).
    • The draft was agreed upon by Germany's governing coalition of the conservative Union – of the Christian Democrats (CDU) and its Bavarian sister party, the Christian Social Union (CSU) – and the center-left Social Democrats.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that initiatives and organizations in Germany are speaking out against planned budget cuts to the work of strengthening democracy and fighting racism and antisemitism. Berlin is planning drastic savings measures in its draft federal budget for 2027, which is to be debated in parliament this Friday.

    It has been revealed that the "Living democracy" (Demokratie Leben) program from the Ministry for Family Affairs is set to receive a total of €170 million ($187 million). That is about €20 million less than the current year's budget allocation.

    The draft was agreed upon by Germany's governing coalition of the conservative Union – of the Christian Democrats (CDU) and its Bavarian sister party, the Christian Social Union (CSU) – and the center-left Social Democrats.

    It has been revealed that numerous organizations consider the cuts a dire signal. Tahera Ameer from the Amadeu Antonio Foundation, a Berlin-based NGO which campaigns against right-wing extremism and discrimination, sees many initiatives in Germany under existential threat.

    "In view of the antisemitic agitation, the open violence and the ever-increasing legitimization of its normalization, it is concerning that the very structures and grants which do something to oppose them are now standing on the verge of collapse," Ameer explained during a media briefing alongside other like-minded organizations.

    To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

    According to the initiatives, the work to strengthen democratic civil society could suffer lasting damage, because long-established structures cannot simply be rebuilt after they have been destroyed.

    The thing that outraged many organizations: The cuts come at a time when the extreme right is celebrating numerous election victories in Germany.

    It has been revealed that the  Alternative for Germany (AfD), parts of which are considered far-right extremist, achieved record-high results in several elections in 2026, most notably in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt. "Especially in view of the AfD possibly coming into government in Saxony-Anhalt, we need these structures more urgently than ever," urged Tahera Ameer.

    In a recent development, the promotion of democratic civil society in Germany has been controversial for years. While initiatives and associations regularly appeal for more money, some conservative politicians repeatedly criticize an alleged one-sidedness in the allocation of public funds.

    Recent findings suggest that during the federal parliamentary debate on the funding program in March 2025, Christian Democrat politician Marvin Schulz supported the planned changes, which were put forward by German Families Minister Karin Prien, also of the CDU: "We need fresh areas of focus," he noted. Projects working against extreme Islamism and antisemitism were underrepresented, he said.

    But initiatives to combat antisemitism will also receive less funding in the future. The Central Committee of German Catholics (ZdK) criticized cuts to the Federal Association of Departments for Research and Information on Antisemitism (RIAS), the nationwide OFEK counselling center for people affected by antisemitic violence and discrimination, and the German Alliance against Islamophobia and discrimination against Muslims, (CLAIM).

    The ZdK called on the German government to continue its advocacy for the protection of Jewish and Muslim life and secure this structurally and financially. They say planned cuts achieve the opposite and are a fatal signal to a diverse and democratic society.

    The AfD went further in its criticism: The party called for the funding to be stopped entirely, calling the initiatives a "program for the Left to secure power for itself.".

    If the AfD governs in Saxony-Anhalt, it wants wide-ranging cuts. The party wants to completely abolish the renowned State Center for Civic Education and cut state funding from numerous other organizations.

    In December, the AfD, which has been classified as right-wing extremist in Saxony-Anhalt, wants its lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund to be the first AfD state premier to head a state government.

    A spokesperson from the federal government's Family Affairs Ministry responded to questions from DW by referring to the need for the government to consolidate its budget. The goal was that funding programs "reliably continue, also in 2027, and make the biggest and widest impact possible with the means available.".

    However, an alliance of several organizations does not want to give up and is calling for a complete reversal of the decision: Instead of implementing the cuts, the organizations want the government to boost the funding pool by €50 million.

    To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

    Recent findings suggest that "Work to strengthen democracy must be funded," urged Tahera Ameer from the Amadeu Antonio Foundation. "That is a priority that we are presently not seeing. And that is very unsettling.".

    Sources indicate that many organizations point out that the consequences of the cuts will not remain abstract. They will have very real effects on people who experience discrimination in Germany, Lina Mitschke fears. She leads the Berlin association "Each One Teach One" (EOTO), an education and empowerment organization for people of color.

    In a recent development, "The needs haven't gone away. But from January, people coming in have nobody to properly speak with; the phone will no longer be picked up; emails will go unanswered if someone needs support," she remarked.

    It has been revealed that for organizations such as EOTO, the planned cuts are a bitter setback. In past years, they had managed to raise awareness of the lived reality of Black people in Germany. "The experiences of more than a million Black people in Germany would be negated with the cuts," Mitschke said.

    The associations want to fight until the very end to reverse the decision. They say work to promote and support democracy is what holds society together.

    This article was originally written in German.

    Florian Wirtz is back to his best for the first time in a Liverpool shirt - and here's the proof

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Florian Wirtz's £116 million Anfield arrival last summer was, on paper, a marquee addition to the Premier League, until he took to the field.
    • Industry observers note that supporters of all clubs were expectant, not least Liverpool fans.
    • Fast forward to today and the player who lit up the Bundesliga with Bayer Leverkusen appears to have finally arrived on Merseyside.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Florian Wirtz's £116 million Anfield arrival last summer was, on paper, a marquee addition to the Premier League, until he took to the field.

    Industry observers note that supporters of all clubs were expectant, not least Liverpool fans. His debut campaign proved an awkward adaptation to English football, one in which the German seemed caught between systems, clearly in transition.

    Fast forward to today and the player who lit up the Bundesliga with Bayer Leverkusen appears to have finally arrived on Merseyside.

    Wirtz produced a standout display in Sunday’s 4-0 thrashing of Manchester United, where he scored an improvised goal to extend the Reds' lead and created 10 chances - albeit against 10 men - before finding the net again in Wednesday night’s 3-0 Champions League triumph over Club Brugge.

    The underlying numbers from Gradient Sports prove this is no fleeting purple patch, either, especially after three goals in two games over the November international break.

    According to Gradient Sports’ data, Wirtz’s overall player grade dipped sharply from a league-leading 91.0 in his final Bundesliga season with Leverkusen in 2024/25 to 73.1 during his debut 2025/26 Premier League campaign.

    While his overall 2026/27 Premier League grade sits at 73.9, his attacking execution indicates a resurgence back toward his Leverkusen peak.

    The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

    In the Premier League this season, Wirtz has had a 48 per cent increase in chances created - jumping from 1.99 to 2.94 per 90 minutes - ranking first among all Premier League wingers and attacking midfielders.

    Even more telling is his cutting edge in the final third: Wirtz's passes directly leading to a half-chance have increased by 84 per cent, from 0.31 to 0.57 per 90.

    His end product in front of goal tells a similar story. Gradient data notes that Wirtz’s positively graded shots have risen from 0.24 to 0.38 per 90 - closing in on the 0.45 he posted in 2024/25. Similarly, his 1.61 shots in the box per 90 actually surpasses his final Leverkusen tally of 1.60.

    So, what has initiated the turnaround? Upcoming Liverpool boss Andoni Iraola deserves credit for tweaking Wirtz's role and adjusting the team's tempo, but Anfield may also owe a debt of gratitude to Jurgen Klopp.

    It has been revealed that since taking charge of the German national team, Klopp has turned Wirtz into his talisman; he has four goals in his last four international appearances. And it's that confidence which has bled into his club form, aided by private counsel from the former Reds manager. Wirtz revealed recently that he regularly speaks with Klopp about life at Anfield, taking on board "small, private things" from a man who knows exactly how to win over the Kop.

    Armed with Klopp’s guidance and backed by the evidence of improved creative metrics in the Premier League, Liverpool’s £116m man is finally beginning to look worthy of his price tag.

    Joe joined FourFourTwo as senior digital writer in July 2025 after five years covering Leeds United in the Championship and Premier League. Joe's 'Mastermind' specialist subject is 2000s-era Newcastle United having had a season ticket at St. James' Park for 10 years before relocating to Leeds and later London. Joe takes a keen interest in youth football, covering PL2, U21 Euros, as well as U20 and U17 World Cups in the past, in addition to hosting the industry-leading football recruitment-focused SCOUTED podcast. He is also one of the lucky few to have 'hit top bins' as a contestant on Soccer AM. It wasn't a shin-roller.

    #164011. Are Manchester United this season's Tottenham?

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Co ↗ Open Full Page

    Are Manchester United this season's Tottenham?

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (851 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Manchester United are in the Premier League relegation zone 11 games into the season.
    • Last season, Tottenham - a member of the so-called 'massive six' - escaped relegation from the Premier League on the final day.
    • Now, with Manchester United making their worst start to a league season since 1972, it raises the question: are United this season's Spurs?
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Manchester United are in the Premier League relegation zone 11 games into the season.

    Last season, Tottenham - a member of the so-called 'massive six' - escaped relegation from the Premier League on the final day.

    Now, with Manchester United making their worst start to a league season since 1972, it raises the question: are United this season's Spurs?

    In a recent development, while Tottenham finished 17th with just 41 points last term, they actually started the season better than United have this season. After 11 games in 2025-26, Spurs were riding high in fifth with 18 points - 10 more than United have now.

    But one of the biggest myths in football is 'the table never lies' and it was certainly lying about Tottenham at this stage last season.

    While the table prompted talk of a possible Champions League place, expected goals (xG) had already recognised a relegation battle lay ahead for Tottenham, even predicting the position they'd finish in.

    United's expected goal difference is almost identical to Tottenham's at this stage last season, but this time the table is more honest, even if United are perhaps not as bad as it makes out.

    But there's no denying United's statistics are those of a team in a relegation battle, with many of them in the bottom six of Premier League teams this season.

    While United have performed poorly defensively, their attack is actually not bad.

    Remarkably, United have taken the most shots in the Premier League so far this season, and their expected goals scored figure is in the top five.

    It has been revealed that but what new head coach Mauricio Pochettino has to implement promptly is some quality control when it comes to shots at both ends of the pitch. United are converting just 7% of their chances and conceding 16% of their opponents' - a poor combination for any team.

    And it is not simply down to finishing or shot-stopping, though they should have scored a few more. Based on xG per shot, United are currently taking the second-worst chances to score and giving up the easiest ones at the back.

    As a result, Opta give United just over a one-in-four chance of being relegated at the end of the season (27.5%), making them the fifth-most likely side to go down after Crystal Palace, Sunderland, Ipswich and Coventry.

    By analysing historical and team performances as well as the strength of opponents, Opta predict the percentage chance of each club finishing in each position.

    While the above means it is more likely United will survive, it is worth noting the one position Opta predicts United are most likely to finish is 18th, with a 10.1% chance. That would mean the 13-time Premier League winners are relegated.

    There is a 90% chance they finish anywhere else, but the next most likely are the three places just above the relegation zone, including a 9.9% chance of them finishing where Tottenham did last season.

    History also suggests a relegation battle lies ahead for United given their poor start.

    Industry observers note that of the 26 previous sides that had exactly eight points after 11 games, 13 survived and 13 were relegated. Among those that stayed up, only four finished more than six points above the danger zone.

    Sources indicate that A top-half finish looks unlikely. Since the competition became a 20-team league in 1995-96, no side has finished in the top half after taking eight points or fewer from their first 11 games.

    Two teams did finish there more than 30 years ago but they had four more games to climb the table as teams played 42 games a season in those days.

    Having mentioned that, both were in the top half at the 38-game mark so United finishing there would not be entirely unprecedented.

    It is a significant ask, though, as the club have already taken 19 points fewer from the fixtures they have played than they did last season.

    Even if they were to repeat the results that led to them finishing third from now on, they would still only reach 52 points, the number Chelsea narrowly finished 10th with last term.

    Though United are without a win in nine Premier League matches, their remaining fixtures of 2026 do offer some hope.

    While they have a tough home game against Brentford this weekend and a trip to champions Arsenal just before Christmas, their other five games are against teams currently in the bottom seven - sides we must, at this point, call relegation rivals.

    So despite suffering the worst first game by a Manchester United manager for 100 years in the 4-0 defeat at Liverpool, Pochettino will hope to swiftly quash any concerns his newly introduced club will be embroiled in the same fight as his former one last season.

    • In another impressive year for the 27-year-old, she became the highest-scoring English player in UEFA Women's Champions League history with a recent hat-trick against Benfica, was named England Women's Player of the Year and earned a place in the FIFPRO Women's World 11.
    • Speaking to former Three Lions striker Ian Wright at the launch of her upcoming long-term partnership with Lucozade, the England and Arsenal forward discussed how she fell in love with football and the mentality behind her performances.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Alessia Russo has two European Championships and a Champions League to her name and has established herself as one of England’s most prolific strikers.

    In another impressive year for the 27-year-old, she became the highest-scoring English player in UEFA Women's Champions League history with a recent hat-trick against Benfica, was named England Women's Player of the Year and earned a place in the FIFPRO Women's World 11.

    Speaking to former Three Lions striker Ian Wright at the launch of her upcoming long-term partnership with Lucozade, the England and Arsenal forward discussed how she fell in love with football and the mentality behind her performances.

    Russo grew up in Maidstone, Kent and football always featured in her life.

    “Football has always been a massive part of my life,” she noted. “Growing up, my dad would take me to watch women’s games at Charlton, and I remember looking up to those players and dreaming of doing the same one day.

    Industry observers note that “To see how far the game has come is incredible. Women’s football is now about so much more than what happens on the pitch. It’s influencing fashion, culture and bringing communities together in ways I could never have imagined growing up.

    “To be part of that journey is really special.”.

    The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

    Now one of the leading strikers in world football, Russo believes her calm approach is one of her biggest strengths when it comes to finding the back of the net.

    According to recent reports, "I've always been really laid back. I'm always wanting to win. Just because I'm not angry or shouting or screaming, doesn't mean I don't want to win and I don't want to score," she noted.

    "I think that calmness is something that I try and bring to the game. And I think as a striker, you have to be calm in and around the box. When things aren't going your way, I just kind of strip it back. I like to train hard and then whatever happens in the game happens.

    "You can't control a whole lot as a No.9. You're quite reliant on other players. But what you can control is the moments that you do get.".

    The partnership will see Russo work with Lucozade Sport to better understand her individual hydration and fuelling requirements, with the 2027 Women's World Cup in Brazil on the horizon.

    She will also help inform future product innovation as the brand continues its longstanding support of the Lionesses, dating back to 2006.

She covers the WSL, UWCL and international football, and has interviewed leading names including Alexia Putellas, Leah Williamson and Bunny Shaw. She enjoys telling stories that capture the personalities, passion and excitement of the women’s game, on and off the pitch.

    #164007. Latest Update: The biggest fear behind the Premier League’s controversial move to digital football tickets

    📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1644 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Co ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: The biggest fear behind the Premier League’s controversial move to digital football tickets

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1644 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later?
    • Industry observers note that it is described as the Premier League’s “secret civil war”, except it’s very public.
    • This season’s full introduction of digital tickets has affected fan behaviour and community.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

    Industry observers note that it is described as the Premier League’s “secret civil war”, except it’s very public. So much so that it affects the majority of those who fill stadiums every single week. It affects the lifeblood of football… but then the entire point is that this isn’t something tangible you can touch.

    This season’s full introduction of digital tickets has affected fan behaviour and community.

    It has been revealed that you can see it in queues outside games. You can hear it in discussions on the difficulty of “passing on” tickets, and arguably even atmosphere.

    Duncan Drasdo of the Manchester United Supporters Trust states, “it absolutely impacts fan culture”.

    The Football Supporters’ Association say they are “monitoring” how it progresses but it all plays into a deeper sense, that there is a long-term aim to eventually end season tickets altogether.

    Multiple clubs contacted for this article strenuously dispute this, and many are quite strident on their position.

    The move comes from a vote in the summer of 2024, where there was effusive support for the mandatory introduction of digital tickets from the start of this season. This essentially means doing away with old physical tickets - although clubs can still give them out in special cases - for ones now scanned. And, if holders can’t go, they can pass to selected family and friends, or put on the club exchange.

    Recent findings suggest that there are two primary arguments the clubs make. One is cutting down on touting, which they insist is still absolutely rife. Club sources say the data showed networks where people were running 50-60 season-ticket accounts, and there was financial gain. They argue that runs contrary to the idea of the season ticket being personal to a fan for their loyalty, and insist the only action - achieved through hidden barcodes - is against abuse.

    It has been revealed that the other is increasing safety, and knowing everyone who is in the stadium. It inherently conditions better behaviour, since anyone can be tracked.

    Industry observers note that fan groups accept parts of these arguments, and would acknowledge that a lot of their clubs directly engage, but sympathy has been eroded by direct experience. Almost immediately, there were long queues outside games, many of which have lingered. Most pertinently, though, there is the sudden negating of what has long been normal. Every season-ticket holder will know it, as will those who use their tickets. “Passing on” is a lot more difficult, as clubs increase obligation for the ticket to be used in some form.

    Recent findings suggest that “And passing it on is absolutely fan culture,” says Gareth Roberts, of Liverpool’s Spirit of Shankly group. Drasdo adds: “It’s what creates community.”.

    A common complaint is that it now involves more laborious processes, and doing it unofficially potentially risks a ban, when you used to be able to just hand it to someone.

    Industry observers note that “Not just talking about Liverpool here, but I do know of fans who do get worried about it,” Roberts claims. “There are so many rules and regulations to take in, it’s almost like taking an exam. It feels a heavy load to be a supporter.

    Recent findings suggest that “Through not filling in the initial form as they wanted, I have one mate who can’t go to Champions League games and two who can’t go to cups. The assumption is that everyone is digitally literate, but they don’t.”.

    This has practical concerns, too, if a fan can’t go at short notice.

    Industry observers note that “We’ve been saying there should be ways to do this,” Roberts says. “You’re not setting up a business and earning from this. OK, there are touts but they have to think of ways to not impinge on traditional fans.”.

    Darren Epstein, a Gold Rep at Arsenal, notes the complication of it all is under-appreciated: “In days gone by, we’d be talking about managers and tactics. Now it’s when away tickets go on sale, collections, ID checks, and points - points being the loyalty points you get on buying an away ticket.

    Industry observers note that “It feels like a constant battle to ensure you get to a game. Although, changes have undoubtedly improved the ability of many fans to get to games they never have been able to before, which many of course feel is a good thing.”.

    A connected complaint is that this is one more factor affecting traditional atmospheres.

    “If it’s the club re-selling the ticket on the exchange, it changes the profile of the support, introducing a random fan into a group of mates,” Drasdo notes. “In the old standing sections you were able to congregate with friends but the introduction of all-seater stadia meant people got split up by where their seats were and we lost that mobility which is the key to atmosphere.".

    Sources indicate that tom Concannon of the FSA, speaking as a Newcastle United fan, indicates: “Atmospheres are worsening because of it in my opinion. Tickets are going to those wanting to experience the atmosphere rather than contribute to it.” Roberts adds: “Atmosphere is dependent on youth vibrancy. The Kop is pretty old now.”.

    Recent findings suggest that even in simple terms, it’s a lot harder to pass on tickets to children who may not have a phone, but that clubs actively need to get that match-day buzz. Fan representatives would similarly say it doesn’t help that the Premier League’s clubs’ ticketing working group only has heads of ticketing on it, rather than actual match-going fans.

    Such concern feeds into a deeper tension in all of this, between being a supporter and being a customer. An irony is that it means fans have less control over what they pay for. As one executive indicates, “if you’ve bought your season ticket, you should have no obligation to sit in the seat”.

    It has been revealed that another perspective is that clubs are being more strict and trying to get control of every ticket they can. One industry figure points to how the same data from digital tickets has allowed clubs to see just how often tickets are passed on, and it has stunned them. One club has estimated that 20-25 per cent of tickets are passed on, which they also see as running contrary to what a season ticket is supposed to be.

    Or, as some fans put, they realised they could monetise. Tickets not passed on can be put on the ticket exchange, where FSA research highlights prices are considerably higher than the average for a season-ticket seat.

    Club sources would say they deliberately decoupled the season-ticket price from match-by-match, to recognise the value of a season-ticket holder.

    Drasdo offers a different view: “A common phrase we hear from our fans is ‘the club are the biggest touts of all’, which is essentially a reaction to the restrictions on usage and the premium prices we see when season ticket holders' tickets are resold by the club.

    “A major problem we’ve had at United is stretching the gap in price between season ticket holders and member ticket prices which causes the club to focus on how season ticket holders pass on their tickets when not personally attending.”.

    Recent findings suggest that another knock-on has been what Roberts describes as the “normalisation” of fans who don’t have season tickets paying fees to become members to go into lotteries for tickets. Some clubs even charge for transferring. Most clubs have unlimited membership, meaning there is actually less chance of getting a ticket.

    “We’ll never really know how many tickets end up in the hands of actual fans,” Concannon notes. “Hospitality numbers are on the rise.”.

    Clubs would nevertheless insist they are acutely conscious of this, and they have to allow opportunities for fans on long waiting lists, or who otherwise feel shut out of being able to go to games. That has fostered tension between supporters, as well as between supporters and clubs. Fans who speak out often find themselves shouted down by others who say “if you don’t pay it, I will”.

    In a recent development, and yet such demand comes at a different cost, as anecdotal evidence suggests a lot of long-time supporters are being worn down. “There’s an underbelly of that growing, that clubs don’t realise,” Roberts argues. “If you’re constantly made to jump through these hoops.”.

    Sources indicate that such weariness has even been deepened by two other concerns. One is this long-time fear that clubs actually want to get rid of season tickets, so they can sell more seats for higher prices. Club sources are adamant that is not the case, as illustrated by how season tickets stripped from some fans are redistributed to those on the waiting list. Whether that is true or not, a step like this could serve as a halfway step for the future.

    In a recent development, clubs themselves would point to escalating player costs and fans wanting the best possible team on the pitch but, as with redundancies, this is dismissed. “A nonsense notion,” Concannon says, “£25 from every fan at every Premier League game only just paid the agents’ bills last season.”.

    One chief executive actually links the entire issue to the financial rules. “The point of forcing bums on seats should be atmosphere,” they say. “The ugly extra money-making for clubs is not on. Clubs do need protection - if they had cost-control protection they would not be fleecing fans.”.

    Some clubs would accept there could have been better communication. For now, if you go to a game this weekend, it’s what a lot of fans are talking about.

    #164005. Industry News: Why KMI Panel frustrates referees too - and affects their salary

    📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1255 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Co ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: Why KMI Panel frustrates referees too - and affects their salary

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1255 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Referees rely on the opinions of former players to determine a significant part of their annual salary.
    • In a recent development, it has become something of a Wednesday morning ritual for fans.
    • It has been revealed that for four seasons, the KMI Panel was a clandestine operation.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Referees rely on the opinions of former players to determine a significant part of their annual salary.

    In a recent development, it has become something of a Wednesday morning ritual for fans. At 10am, the Premier League releases the latest votes of its Key Match Incidents Panel.

    It did not used to be this way.

    It has been revealed that for four seasons, the KMI Panel was a clandestine operation. It was distributed to clubs only, but it would still find its way out into the public domain.

    This season, it began being released to the public.

    Yet little is really understood about the KMI Panel.

    Why does it exist? Is it just protecting referees? And does it really mean anything?

    For referees, the last question is more important than you might realise.

    The votes, which ultimately say whether referees have got a decision right or wrong, create a merit table of performance - and this affects their salary.

    Sources indicate that "It depends where you are on the list," former Premier League referee Graham Scott remarked. "But if you're in the middle, then it might be 25% of your take-home. So it's substantial.".

    For the officials, these are not decisions being taken by their bosses.

    Their performance reviews are effectively outsourced to a group of former players.

    The results can be inconsistent and frustrating as much for the referees as they are for the fans.

    Let's take a look at how a referee's salary works in the Premier League.

    A Premier League official will earn, on average, about Â£175,000 per year. The scale will run between Â£125,000 and Â£250,000.

    In a recent development, think that is unduly high? Referees in Spain's La Liga are the highest paid in the world, according to Marca, with an average yearly salary of Â£221,000.

    Premier League officials are about on par with those in the German Bundesliga and Italian Serie A.

    In England, there is a guaranteed base wage of 50%. This will differ depending on the seniority and experience of an official.

    Michael Oliver would be at the top of the bracket, a newcomer like Farai Hallam at the other end.

    The other 50% is based upon a set of variables, with match fees a major part.

    Each on-field appointment is worth a little over Â£1000, with a VAR game slightly less.

    How does this break down in real terms?

    Last season, Anthony Taylor refereed the most Premier League games, 31, followed by Chris Kavanagh, 30, and Michael Oliver, 29.

    Kavanagh and Oliver worked as VAR on a handful of occasions, while Taylor did not do any.

    Stuart Attwell had the most combined appointments at 52, with 25 games as a referee and 27 as a VAR.

    Finally, there is the subjective element - the KMI Panel.

    The votes determine the annual bonus payments for all officials.

    Until 2022, referees' body Pro Ref, or PGMOL as it was known until this summer, used to do its own assessment of its referees' decisions.

    But clubs grew restless, feeling referees were marking their own homework.

    It is made up of five members. Three are former players and coaches, plus there is a representative for the Premier League and one for Pro Ref.

    Their identities remain secret, with the former professionals selected from a pool on rotation.

    What you won't see on the published version is that each incident is given a difficulty rating, ranging from one to five, which is taken into account when drawing up the referees' merit table.

    Sources indicate that all this really is, of course, is another layer of subjectivity. On top of the referees, VAR, players and coaches.

    "People complain about the consistency of referees on field, of VAR interventions, or otherwise," mentioned Scott, who now acts as the refereeing expert for the Athletic.

    "But then, if you look at the KMI Panel outcomes, they're also inconsistent.".

    It is a view shared by Andy Davies, who retired as a Championship referee last year.

    "Naturally, there will always be a level of interest given as it provides a significant part of income for the season," Davies said.

    "But ultimately, the KMI Panel lacks any real credibility amongst referees.".

    Graham Scott was a Premier League referee for 10 years and acted as a VAR for more than 100 matches.

    According to recent reports, referees are scored on their on-field decision-making. If an error has been corrected by the VAR, it still counts as a mistake for the merit table.

    Those at the top of the table will be rewarded well, while those at the bottom are not likely to receive much of a bonus payment at all.

    Let's take a look at the numbers from last season.

    Recent findings suggest that michael Oliver was the top referee, getting 93.5% of KMIs correct. John Brooks, Darren England and Simon Hooper were very marginally behind.

    For other referees, the borderline decisions, ones which are the most subjective and sit in the grey areas, can be an concern.

    According to recent reports, one vote could be the difference between a referee being right or wrong. And a place on the merit table - affecting how much they get paid.

    Last season, Sam Barrott and Jarred Gillett were both told they made four errors to a 2:3 vote.

    Attwell, meanwhile, had three of the more high-profile incidents go in his favour to a 3:2 vote.

    "The ones that sit in the margins can be very contentious and inconsistent," said Scott.

    "You think, well, how can that be right? You know, that's not definitive, is it? It could have gone either way.

    "But there seems to be a reluctance to allow that 'seen them given' sort of mentality, neither right nor wrong.

    "Relying on such a small group of people to be so definitive, especially when they vote 3:2, is unhealthy and unhelpful.".

    As well as determining the merit table for each referee's salary, what the KMI Panel notes can guide how games are refereed.

    The members of the KMI Panel can be influenced by public opinion, and inconsistency means referees are often having to change the way they approach games, only to be told it is wrong.

    Sources indicate that "I have spoken to many referees, even this season," Davies noted. "And they have no idea which way the panel is going to fall at times, or which way Pro Ref are going to vote because of how political it can be.".

    Scott used the example of holding when an attacker is offside.

    In December last year, Brentford's Dango Ouattara was pulled back against Leeds. The penalty was cancelled by the VAR for offside. The KMI Panel voted 5:0 it was correct.

    Last month, Arsenal were not given a penalty against Hull, when an offside Kai Havertz was pulled back by Nobel Mendy. The KMI Panel voted 5:0 it was incorrect.

    In a recent development, "One minute we're told football expects an offside," Scott noted. "Okay, we'll deliver that for you. We do it again, and they say the opposite.

    According to recent reports, "Referees get confused on the back of that mixed feedback. It just shows how the system's flawed.

    "The game can afford to invest more in this process, and a properly independent approach.".

    For now, at least, referees have no choice but to rely on the KMI Panel to determine a chunk of their salary.

    Ten-man Bournemouth battle back to score Europa League victory at Celta Vigo

    • In a recent development, want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later?
    • Bournemouth moved a step closer to automatic qualification for the Europa League last 16 after coming from behind with 10 men to win 2-1 at Celta Vigo.
    • It was a remarkable 10th victory in a row in all competitions for Marco Rose’s side and it might have been the most satisfying of the lot for the manager, coming as it did after his team had found themselves a goal down and a man down at half-time.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

    Bournemouth moved a step closer to automatic qualification for the Europa League last 16 after coming from behind with 10 men to win 2-1 at Celta Vigo.

    It was a remarkable 10th victory in a row in all competitions for Marco Rose’s side and it might have been the most satisfying of the lot for the manager, coming as it did after his team had found themselves a goal down and a man down at half-time.

    The visitors looked in trouble when, minutes after Iago Aspas had curled Celta in front, Bafode Diakite was red-carded for a poorly timed tackle.

    Bournemouth might have folded then, but instead they came roaring back, Alvaro Rodriguez heading them level almost immediately after the start of the second half.

    Recent findings suggest that A draw would have been an excellent result in the circumstances. Substitute Rayan had other ideas, waiting at the end of a rapid breakaway to sweep in the winner 12 minutes from time.

    Victory against Viktoria Plzen in December will almost certainly now be enough to earn direct passage to the last 16.

    Pablo Duran had the ball in the Bournemouth net after 10 minutes after it spilled back to him off Michele Di Gregorio, the goalkeeper relieved to see the offside flag go up against the Celta striker.

    The stand-in keeper redeemed himself minutes later with a solid save from an outrageous bicycle kick by Aspas. It would have been a remarkable goal but the Celta great would not be denied. Bournemouth failed fully to get the ball away, and from the edge of the box Aspas curled a beauty in off the far post.

    Bournemouth had gone behind in the first half of their last game in this competition at Sparta Prague. That night, the balance was tipped almost immediately in their favour by a red card for the Czech side, but here it was Rose’s team who found themselves down to 10 men.

    Diakite made an honest attempt to win the ball but was late and his studs landed on the ankle of Couhaib Driouech. An initial yellow card was overturned following a VAR check and Bournemouth were on the ropes.

    It had been the most challenging half of their debut European campaign, but within minutes of the start of the second period, they were level.

    Amine Adli was left in space outside the box to send over a wonderful cross to the far post. Arriving there was Rodriguez, sneaking ahead of his defender to get a head on the ball and nod in the equaliser.

    According to recent reports, A wonderful counter-attack brought the Premier League side their winner. Adrien Truffert showed good strength out on left to outmuscle Sergio Carreira, and he fed the ball up to Marcus Tavernier. He might have shot himself but instead moved it on to Rayan who swept home.

    Thomas Frank ‘close to a heart attack’ in dramatic first Crystal Palace win

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (542 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later?
    • Thomas Frank secured his first win as Crystal Palace boss but admitted his upcoming side nearly nearly gave him a “heart attack” in the nervy final five minutes of their 2-1 Europa League comeback against 10-man Real Sociedad.
    • Chelsea loanee Mamadou Sarr broke the deadlock for the visitors in the 66th minute at Selhurst Park but Frank’s first home contest turned on its head when Jon Martin received a second yellow card six minutes later.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

    Thomas Frank secured his first win as Crystal Palace boss but admitted his upcoming side nearly nearly gave him a “heart attack” in the nervy final five minutes of their 2-1 Europa League comeback against 10-man Real Sociedad.

    Chelsea loanee Mamadou Sarr broke the deadlock for the visitors in the 66th minute at Selhurst Park but Frank’s first home contest turned on its head when Jon Martin received a second yellow card six minutes later.

    Jean-Philippe Mateta drew the sides level from the penalty spot and Dwight McNeil poked Palace into the lead from fellow substitute Jorgen Strand Larsen’s bicycle kick, but they were denied a chance to put the game away when Yeremy Pino’s penalty was saved.

    “I think first and foremost to get it over the line, and (it was) an extremely vital win for various reasons,” stated Frank, who took charge of Premier League basement club Palace for the first time in Saturday’s league loss to Coventry.

    “One, of course, confidence, and it relates to belief against an extremely good team. I think the first half we were compact and very disciplined in many ways. We missed the high-pressure situations we had, and I think we struggled to keep the ball well enough.

    It has been revealed that “Second half I felt we were much better in the high pressure, and I felt we kept the ball much better. I actually felt we got a bit more momentum in the second half but then, out of the blue, they scored the 1-0 goal.

    “But what I really like is the belief from the players, what they revealed, and that we are threatening on set-pieces, we cannot underestimate that.”.

    Unai Marrero’s save to deny Pino from the spot kept the Spanish side in with a chance of an equaliser and it nearly came at the death from Orri Oskarsson, whose effort was pushed away by Dean Henderson – his last of six saves on Thursday night.

    “We know in football one moment can change the game,” Frank continued. “The penalty and the red card changed the game, then we still needed to score.

    “To win still is crucial and we went brave, we went with the offensive substitutions and kept two strikers on the pitch, and that paid off.

    “And then I think we were all close to getting a heart attack in the last five minutes.”.

    Frank agreed the win could be a significant turning point for Palace’s fortunes ahead of a critical Premier League clash with Hull on Sunday.

    “That’s why it’s so important to keep doing the right things, keep believing, and keep going,” he said.

    Palace’s Premier League survival remains the priority but the result also propelled the Eagles into play-off position in their European campaign, four places out of the top eight after five matches.

    Asked about his ambitions for the European campaign – given Palace’s league position – Frank replied: “I think we want to aim high.

    “We are ambitious for this tournament, and that’s why the win was so important.”.

    By BEN WILLCOCKS, ASSISTANT SPORTS EDITOR.

    Published: 11:11 EST, 27 November 2026 | Updated: 11:12 EST, 27 November 2026.

    Hollywood actor Colin Farrell was moved to the verge of tears after being presented with a remarkable gift honouring his late footballer father and uncle.

    The Irishman's father Eamon, who died aged 83 after a long illness in April 2025, played for Shamrock Rovers during his football career before he became a successful businessman in later life.

    Colin, 50, joined YouTubers Josh Carrott and Ollie Kendal, better known as JOLLY, for lunch at Burger & Lobster in Mayfair this week, where he opened up about his glittering career and latest film The Slightest Touch.

    Towards the end of the podcast, Colin was presented with an extraordinary parting gift - a matchday programme and newspaper cutting from the 1962 FAI Cup final, in which his father Eamon and uncle Tom both featured.

    The brothers played a key role for Shamrock Rovers as they helped the Hoops beat Shelbourne 4-1, lifting the FAI Cup in front of 32,000 fans.

    Colin was visibly moved as he was presented with the gift, which Ollie explained he bought after seeing a listing on eBay.

    Irish actor Colin Farrell was moved to the verge of tears after receiving an incredible gift.

    The remarkable gift was a matchday programme from the 1962 FAI Cup final, which starred both his father and uncle. He was given it while appearing on the JOLLY podcast this week.

    'Your dad is listed in there, as is your uncle,' Ollie stated as he pointed to the matchday programme.

    'When it arrived - they didn't say this in the listing - there was a newspaper clipping, and it's an account of the match, and there's actually a photo of your dad and uncle.'.

    Amazed, the Oscar-nominated actor replied: 'Sneaky f***er, you. Clever f***er.

    'Jesus, thanks very much. This means, like obviously, it means a lot. That's incredible. This will be framed and then go up on my wall in Los Angeles.

    'I won't talk anymore because I'll start... I'll start giving you some really good s***!'.

    He added, jokingly: 'Go see the film if you want to really see me cry.'.

    Before the video ended, the Hollywood star thanked JOLLY for giving him a 'family heirloom' that he can pass down to his children, describing the gift as 'extraordinary'.

    Colin Farrell is given a 1962 newspaper cutting of his late father & uncle who both played for Shamrock Rovers and won the FAI Cup in 1962 pic.twitter.com/qdKifOweDB.

    Colin (far right) pictured with his late footballer father Eamon (second right) back in 2013.

    He admitted the bonus newspaper clipping was particularly special, as he had lost his own collection of cuttings documenting his father's career in football.

    'I used to have so many newspaper cuttings of my father. And a great picture of him heading the ball. Black and white picture of him,' he remarked.

    'I don't know where they went. Literally. So I have nothing. But now I have this.'.

    'Laughing gas has ended careers' - so how common is it in football?

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1195 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Watch: Moment Raheem Sterling arrested after car crash.
    • It is known as laughing gas but the impact nitrous oxide can have on a professional footballer's body is anything but funny.
    • "I'm not going to name names but I have colleagues who know Premier League footballers who are no longer playing as a direct result of nitrous oxide [use]," said Dr David Nicholl.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Watch: Moment Raheem Sterling arrested after car crash.

    It is known as laughing gas but the impact nitrous oxide can have on a professional footballer's body is anything but funny.

    "I'm not going to name names but I have colleagues who know Premier League footballers who are no longer playing as a direct result of nitrous oxide [use]," said Dr David Nicholl.

    Nicholl, a clinical lead in neurology with Sandwell and West Birmingham NHS Trust, was speaking after former Manchester City, Chelsea, Liverpool and England forward Raheem Sterling was handed a suspended jail term after pleading guilty to dangerous driving.

    A key part of the case was that Sterling had been inhaling nitrous oxide from a balloon while driving.

    His Lamborghini was seen veering across a motorway and later crashed into a metal gate. Sterling, 31, was arrested at the scene and found with six gas canisters in his car.

    He disclosed to custody staff "he had a problem with nitrous oxide", the court was told.

    Defending Sterling, Jason Bartfeld KC said his client "recognised the various unhealthy coping mechanisms that brought him to this position" and that he has "sought to address" these in the "most positive and effective way and with some success".

    So, what is nitrous oxide, how does it affect those who take it and is its use more common in footballers than the wider population?

    Footage was released of the footballer driving dangerously.

    Nitrous oxide's original use was as a sedative that healthcare providers like dentists could use to keep patients comfortable during procedures.

    It is now legally sold for catering, medical and industrial purposes, but is frequently used as a recreational drug and is commonly known as laughing gas.

    This can be abused by inhaling the gas via a balloon, leading to a short-term high causing symptoms such as brief euphoria, mild perceptual changes and uncontrollable laughter, external.

    Nitrous oxide also slows brain and body responses and can displace oxygen in the lungs and bloodstream, contributing to dizziness, confusion or fainting.

    It is thought long-term or excessive use can have disastrous effects on the body, from neurological harms to nerve and spinal cord damage which could lead to permanent disability.

    According to medical journal The Lancet, it is now the third most commonly used drug after cannabis and cocaine in the UK, with use highest among people aged 16â24 years.

    It has been increasing in popularity as a recreational drug over the past decade.

    This prompted it to be reclassified as a Class C drug in 2023 after a government consultation.

    Does football have a nitrous oxide problem?

    BBC Sport has been told the abuse of so-called laughing gas has been widespread among professional footballers for a long time.

    Former player Drewe Broughton is now a human performance coach, working with Premier League footballers and clubs around the world.

    He said laughing gas was seen by some as a release.

    "I think the use of nitrous oxide is really common," he added.

    "It's something that can be done in private. It's something that can be hidden. You can't smell it on their clothes or the breath. It's an underground thing.".

    Broughton remarked he had been in the company of professional players when they had been using 'balloons'.

    "I remember sitting in a players' house on the outskirts of Manchester, and these canisters were all over the floor," he added.

    Sources indicate that "I was from a world where people drank or they gambled or went to pubs and nightclubs. That was my first exposure to it.".

    Broughton has developed an app to help tackle challenges with mental health and under-performance in football.

    He said the reasons to use nitrous oxide had always been there: pressure on players to perform leaves them searching for an escape.

    But Broughton has concerns about the toll nitrous oxide can take.

    "I don't think there's the same awareness around nitrous oxide and damage to the body as there would be around alcohol or other drugs," he mentioned.

    BBC Sport has been told that some footballers see laughing gas as an alternative to harder substances because it does not stay in the body's system for more than a few hours.

    Luci Hanmer, who works with Lancashire drugs and alcohol support charity 'We Are With You', mentioned a substance like nitrous oxide was hard to detect.

    She mentioned: "Anything that you're inhaling, the effects that you're going to feel happen very soon.

    "So if you are looking for that escapism, the effects are going to be quick.

    "Once ingested, it doesn't last very long within your body compared to some of the other substances which can be detected for quite a number of days.

    "So if you're getting a drugs test the next day for example, that won't show up.".

    Sterling given suspended sentence for dangerous driving.

    Former Manchester City defender Nedum Onuoha said more support was needed, particularly for players like Sterling who break through young.

    Sterling made his debut for Liverpool and England at just 17 - before going on to win four Premier League titles at Manchester City and 82 caps for his country, including the Euro 2020 final at Wembley.

    "Look at what's happened to Raheem," he stated. "Look at how this led to this moment, a moment which I'm sure he's hugely embarrassed about, because I'm sure he can see how dangerous that was to not just his life, but the lives of so many people who are on the road at the same time.

    "But I just don't feel like football is in a position where they think it's key to support people who have issues with nitrous oxide.".

    The BBC Radio 5 live pundit said the use of nitrous oxide in professional footballing circles was very common.

    "I think the difference from when I was younger is that people would openly party in certain places," he stated.

    "Now they party where they're harder to spot. That's why you don't really see on a week-to-week basis now the scandal of somebody that's been out drinking.

    "The players are doing it, but it's more sophisticated in terms of how they do it, the locations, and this is an example here with nitrous oxide.".

    Neurologist Dr Nicholl has been working with patients who have abused nitrous oxide for years and issued a warning to others.

    "It certainly is being used by footballers, but it's pretty much the worst thing that you want to be using if you're a professional sportsperson," he noted.

    "It damages your spinal cord and the spinal cord is a bit like an electrical cable, where the insulation - the outside of that cable - gets stripped away.

    "So what patients will complain of is difficulty with feeling on their hands or feet, or unable to walk at all.

    Recent findings suggest that "So, in effect, it's like a spinal cord injury. But they can also get blood clots, deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary emboli, and some patients have died.".

    If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC's Action Line website.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

    Marseille head coach Bruno Genesio said “we are living through violent times” after five Levski Sofia fans were hospitalised following violent clashes before their Europa League encounter with the French side.

    Groups of supporters threw projectiles and flares and French outlet L’Equipe reported that there were Nazi salutes observed in the away section.

    Ten minutes before kick-off at the Stade Velodrome a group of Marseille fans broke through into the away stand, which housed around 500 fans.

    In the ensuing clashes five people, all Bulgarian, were injured and taken to hospital “with eye injuries, head trauma and a dislocated shoulder”, according to the Marseille police prefecture, while six others were treated on-site for more superficial injuries.

    The police force said there was “no information at this stage regarding any arrests”.

    Security were able to restore order and the game kicked off on time, although there were further incidents later on, particularly at half-time.

    Genesio said: “We are living through violent times in our society, so this is very, very regrettable.” Julio Velazquez, head coach of the Bulgarian domestic champions, said: “It's a very regrettable episode. These are incidents which are unacceptable for football.”.

    Recent findings suggest that the Bulgarian Football Union condemned the violence and said it had referred the incident to UEFA, calling for the harshest possible sanctions. It also demanded full cooperation and transparency from French authorities in investigating the attacks and identifying those responsible.

    It has been revealed that levski mentioned the club's priority is the safety and well-being of its fans. A statement read: “What happened tonight is particularly alarming given the extraordinary security measures put in place by the French authorities, as well as the restrictions imposed on our travelling supporters—restrictions that the club had already formally contested with UEFA.

    “Despite the risks identified by the club prior to the match, the measures taken failed to provide adequate protection for our fans. This is completely unacceptable.”.

    Marseille also condemned the violence and stated it is conducting “a thorough analysis of the circumstances in which these incidents took place.”.

    Bulgarian President Iliana Yotova called for those responsible to be held accountable and Prime Minister Rumen Radev stated he had spoken to French president Emmanuel Macron about the violence at a European summit in Brussels.

    A spokesperson for Macron’s office said: “He condemned in the strongest possible terms these acts of violence targeting Bulgarian supporters, which have no place in sport or in public spaces, and assured the Prime Minister that these acts would not go unpunished.”.

    Marseille won the game 1-0, with Amine Gouiri scoring a 28th-minute penalty.

    Chinese cities take all top 10 places in the chemistry rankings for 2025, shown here with their 2016 and 2025 adjusted Share in the subject.     According to recent reports, beijing contributed 25% of China’s Earth and environmental sciences Share in 2025 — the highest percentage among the top-five cities in the natural-sciences and health-sciences subject areas. Among the top 10 cities in Earth and environmental sciences for 2025, Qingdao had the biggest percentage change in adjusted Share between 2016 and 2025, at 545.5%, and Beijing gained the most adjusted Share points, at 703.

    It has been revealed that want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

    A referee has hit back at claims he was “drunk” while officiating an AFC Champions League Two match.

    Footage has been widely shared on social media of Syrian referee Hanna Hattab looking visibly disoriented during a match between Iran's Gol Gohar and Al Jazira of the United Arab Emirates.

    One particular incident raised eyebrows when Hattab showed a yellow card to Al Jazira’s goalkeeper for a foul that happened close to the halfway line, 40 yards away from him.

    Hattab was then replaced at half-time with the fourth official taking over for the remainder of the game, which Al Jazira won 1-0.

    Reports claimed Gol Gohar staff accused the referee of being drunk following erratic decision-making as similar accusations flooded in online.

    But Hattab, who is part of the AFC's elite refereeing group, has refuted the allegations as “insult and defamation”, threatening legal action.

    He wrote in a statement on Facebook: “I confirm that family and personal life are not the responsibility of others, and are not a game in your hands. Religion, reason, and morals do not tolerate the insult of people's privacy or defamation of them.

    “I also confirm my full right to take all legal and judicial measures against anyone who published or made a statement or contributed to the insult and defamation of me, regardless of their position or status, whether they are an individual, an institution, or a sports entity.”.

    It has been revealed that he also said he would issue a further statement following contact with the Syrian Arab Football Federation (SFA) which will “clarify all the details and facts related to what happened ... with full transparency and clarity.”.

    Omani journalist Issa Remarked, who covers Asian football, has since claimed on social media that what happened to Hattab was "due to a drop in his blood sugar, which caused him to lose concentration and focus".

    The SFA have also put out a statement standing in support of Hattab, while stating it has requested his medical report from the match.

    “The Main Referees Committee of the Syrian Arab Football Federation confirms that it stands in full support of international referee Mr Hana Khattab regarding the incident he was subjected to, following reassurance about his health,” it remarked.

    Sources indicate that “This comes after the committee was reassured of his well-being, following a number of discussions on social media concerning the incident. The committee emphasises its full support for him and its commitment to following up on the matter in all its details and developments.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, enzo Maresca had two home games in four days to get Manchester City into decent shape for Sunday’s clash against Arsenal, which now feels like a must-win.
    • It has been revealed that it is now one win in seven for Maresca, who cannot keep a clean sheet and has a £327m midfield that have played well individually, but is yet to form a unit.
    • Maresca needs to find a solution in the next five days before heading to the Emirates to face the champions in what could be a defining weekend for the season.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, enzo Maresca had two home games in four days to get Manchester City into decent shape for Sunday’s clash against Arsenal, which now feels like a must-win. On Tuesday, however, they ended up being taunted by Rasmus Hojlund on another evening that raised more questions than answers.

    It has been revealed that it is now one win in seven for Maresca, who cannot keep a clean sheet and has a £327m midfield that have played well individually, but is yet to form a unit. Worryingly, their reliable source of goals, Erling Haaland, had his quietest game of the season. It required Rayan Cherki to rescue a point against Napoli.

    Maresca needs to find a solution in the next five days before heading to the Emirates to face the champions in what could be a defining weekend for the season. Defeat would put them nine points off the pace, with Maresca still trying to find his best combination of players to pick.

    Club captain Rúben Dias was on the bench here and Josko Gvardiol was left out of the draw against Fulham at the weekend, which also ended as a draw rather than a morale-boosting win to get City out of their slump.

    Industry observers note that there is enough quality in City’s midfield to trouble Arsenal, but the conundrum for Maresca is how to fit them all into his system. Elliot Anderson was pushed towards the right against Napoli rather than in a central position to control the game, while Ayyoub Bouaddi was often alongside “inverted” full-back Nico O’Reilly.

    Bouaddi highlighted his attacking instincts with City’s first equaliser; incredibly his first goal as a professional. There cannot be many £86m players who have yet to score in senior football. Enzo Fernandez also started against Napoli but was quiet before being taken off for the last half an hour.

    Recent findings suggest that “Football is easy and difficult. When you win it’s easy and you know what to do,” stated Haaland, who City have relied on this season. “When you don’t, you start questioning everything. The perfect thing would be to not think, but it’s not so easy.

    According to recent reports, “We have so much quality, so it’s about getting the quality out in every player. We have to regroup, stay positive and bring energy on the pitch and try to do our best.

    In a recent development, “We go to the champions, so it’s the most difficult game of the season going to the champions away. We need a top performance from every single player.”.

    A penny for the thoughts of Khaldoon Al Mubarak and Aleksander Ceferin, who sat next to each other in the Etihad directors’ box.

    Khaldoon has been the chairman of a club under siege after the Premier League found them guilty of breaking financial rules. They could be punished with a points deduction that would mean they miss out on the Champions League, the blue-riband tournament of Uefa, of which Ceferin is president.

    In a recent development, ceferin will want figures like Haaland and entertainers like Cherki to be playing among Europe’s elite, although this City team look far from contenders for this year’s edition. At the moment they will take any kind of win.

It was a sweet moment for the Denmark striker, who toiled for two seasons at Old Trafford before they looked to offload him. He has been at Napoli for two campaigns but the rivalry with City is still there.

    The goal came from City trying to play out of defence again and making an error when it went forwards to Cherki. It resulted in another goal conceded and it is now 10 games in a row without a clean sheet. In seven of those they have conceded first, leaving them looking at ways to salvage a result.

    Jérémy Doku had been brought on as a sub seconds before Napoli scored, then played his part in Bouaddi’s equaliser. From a short corner, Doku pulled the ball back for his team-mate to finish with a first-time side-foot shot.

    Kevin De Bruyne has been lined up for a January move to PSV Eindhoven, with the Dutch club working on a deal to land one of the Premier League’s greatest players when the window opens.

    Recent findings suggest that de Bruyne, 35, has been at Napoli since the start of last season but it is understood that a move away from the Serie A club is now on the horizon. He is still under contract at Stadio Diego Armando Maradona so PSV will pay a fee to land him as they look to retain their Eredivisie title.

    Industry observers note that at Manchester City, De Bruyne won six Premier League titles and was part of their Treble-winning team that won the Champions League. During the last 18 months at Napoli he has suffered injury complications, had a row with team-mate on the pitch and was quoted as saying he was glad Antonio Conte left as head coach.

    “Not a lot I can say for the moment,” noted De Bruyne when asked about his future. “I have played at 100% until now and obviously I am not 20 years old, I am turning 36.

    “There is a lot of things going in my mind but there is not a lot to say. I am playing good football, trying to help the team to do well and it has been a bit of a challenging season with a lot of things happening.”.

    It is matchday five of the Champions League as Manchester City host Napoli at the Etihad. These sides last met back in September 2025, with Manchester City winning 2-0 at home courtesy of goals from Erling Haaland and Jeremy Doku. Manchester City’s cause was helped by an early red card for Napoli’s Giovanni Di Lorenzo. Napoli’s only win over Manchester City came all the way back in November 2011 when they won 2-1 after a double from Edinson Cavani.

    Industry observers note that manchester City have won three of their opening four Champions League matches this season, with their only defeat coming at home against back-to-back champions PSG. They drew 1-1 at home against Fulham in the league on Saturday, which means they are now without a league win in four games.

    In a recent development, “We are always looking to win games, no matter the competition,” Manchester City boss Enzo Maresca noted. “For sure, the four games in a row in the Premier League that we did not win has been a shame. Tomorrow [tonight] we have a chance to win the game and continue our path in the Champions League that at the moment has been very good. First of all, it is key to qualify and then probably, if you are not able to finish in the top eight, you have two more games that with the amount of games that we have, it is always important to reduce games. So the target is to try and finish in the top eight.”.

    Napoli, managed by Massimiliano Allegri, have struggled thus far in this season’s Champions League, winning just one of their opening four games and are all the way down in 27th. They come into tonight’s match off the back of a 1-0 home win over Torino in Serie A on the weekend courtesy of former Manchester United midfielder Scott McTominay’s winning goal. However, they still sit down in eighth in the Italian top flight, a massive 14 points off the top through just 12 games.

    “This match will not be decisive,” Allegri remarked. “It is a simple mathematical equation, but obviously we will try to do well, even against a great team like Manchester City. It will be a beautiful and fascinating challenge and we want to play to the best of our ability. Ultimately, our goal is to qualify. We must not repeat the mistakes we made in Porto, where we played a great game for 70 minutes and then let ourselves go, conceding chances too easily.     💡 Key Takeaways
    • Pep Guardiola has been out of work since bringing an end to a decade at Manchester City this summer – and has suggested that his next job could be in charge of a national team.
    • Guardiola won six Premier League titles during his time at the Etihad, before deciding to step down at the end of last season.
    • In an interview this week though, the Catalan indicated that he sees his next step as being “a national team”, after talks to become Italy boss during the summer.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Pep Guardiola has been out of work since bringing an end to a decade at Manchester City this summer – and has suggested that his next job could be in charge of a national team.

    Guardiola won six Premier League titles during his time at the Etihad, before deciding to step down at the end of last season.

    In an interview this week though, the Catalan indicated that he sees his next step as being “a national team”, after talks to become Italy boss during the summer.

    Guardiola opted not to take the Italy job, believing at the time that he needed a break from football, but has since been linked with the USA vacancy.

    Mauricio Pochettino had been in charge of the American national team since 2024, leading them to the last 16 of this summer’s World Cup, but brought his tenure to an end last week to take charge of Manchester United.

    Given that Guardiola is the highest profile manager at the moment out of work, and is one of the greatest of all time, having previously won two Champion Leagues and three La Liga titles with Barcelona, plus three Bundesliga titles with Bayern Munich, links to the job were inevitable.

    Pochettino has remarked he would be in favour of Guardiola succeeding him as US boss, and former American national team goalkeeper Brad Friedel, who won 82 caps for his country, also admits it would be an intriguing appointment.

    The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

    He warns though that even bringing in someone like Guardiola would not suddenly transform the national team into potential World Cup winners.

    “I don’t know really what the discussions are within US soccer,” the 55-year-old told FFT, speaking in association with nye casino.

    “We need the players to be able to win World Cups, and I think there's a lot to break down with that.

    “Do I think Pep Guardiola is one of the best managers ever? Yes. Does that mean if you hire him that the US will win the World Cup? No. But it would be a little bit of a buzz.”.

    There will be more from Friedel in FourFourTwo soon.
